This page has long been used as an entry point for revisiting `src/managers/GitRefManager.js`. It was kept early on not because refpaths had already been mapped out in full, but because a fixed file was needed as a place to land when path-related clues came up during code reading. The earliest wording was brief: first open GitRefManager, then follow refpaths further. That sentence remained in the previous version and read like a direct navigation suggestion. It did save a round of searching at the time, but it also created a persistent misunderstanding: some people treated the filename as defining the scope of path handling, lumping the entry point, local declarations, and the place where failure ultimately occurred together at the same level.

Old wording: **Finding `GitRefManager.js` means finding where refpaths is handled.**

That statement no longer applies. The file is still a suitable entry point because it brings readers to local objects they can check; however, it cannot replace separate checks of the declarations within the file, direct dependencies, and failure/event exit points. This page is not being expanded into a new overview. Old links continue to point here so that readers see this correction first.

## What to Record at the Entry Point

When starting from the file, first confirm that you are looking at `src/managers/GitRefManager.js`; do not jump to a snippet based only on the text `refpaths` in the search results. The object identified by this filename is GitRefManager; refpaths is one thread to follow when reading that object. Only by listing the two side by side in the notes can we avoid later mistaking the path name for the module name.

The frozen material limits this page's scope to three kinds of local relationships: declarations within the file, their direct dependencies, and the exit points through which failures or events leave the file. The reading notes should also stop at these three kinds of relationships. If you see a name adjacent to a path, first record it as a local declaration; if that name is passed to an object elsewhere for handling, record that hop as a direct dependency. Do not assume in advance that objects encountered later belong inside GitRefManager just because their names are similar.

The following simple diagram can be used for temporary annotations at the entry point:

```text
GitRefManager.js
  |
  +-- Local declarations adjacent to refpaths
  |
  +-- Direct dependencies
  |
  `-- Where failures or events leave the file
```

The absence of specific symbols in the diagram is an old gap deliberately left intact. None of the previous rounds of notes copied the frozen declarations into this page one by one; filling in guessed names would only make this long-standing entry point look more complete than it was at the time. When symbols need to be checked, go directly back to the file itself rather than relying on this old diagram.

## Reading Approaches That Went Wrong

The first notes gave the search order as "refpaths → GitRefManager → caller". That order is not necessarily wrong in itself; the problem is that it omitted the relationships between adjacent objects within the file. As a result, seeing a more distant call site made it easy to treat it as the only source of refpaths, or to treat an error exit point as the end of the entire path logic.

After the second review, the sequence was changed to pause within the file first:

- First identify whether a local declaration actually carries the path-related thread forward;
- Then record the direct dependencies the declaration encounters;
- Only then determine whether the failure or event arises within the file or is propagated out from the dependency side.

This sequence does not provide the final semantics, but it can prevent the most common skipped steps in the old notes. It also explains why the term "handling location" should be removed from this page: the same path-related thread may first be observed within the file, continue across a dependency boundary, and only produce the result visible to the caller on the other side. Calling all three stages the handling location does not help when revisiting the code.

The previous version also described a "path" as though it were a self-contained object. That was a simplification made while reading, not a classification that should be retained here. The current page uses relationships between objects: GitRefManager is the file object, refpaths is the thread for beginning the code reading, declarations and dependencies are adjacent objects that need to be checked individually, and failure or event exit points mark where these notes on the file stop. Writing it this way does not replace further code reading; it only avoids compounding the misunderstanding at this old entry point.

## How to Revisit the Code Now

When you need to investigate historical behavior, first open `GitRefManager.js` and read in source order, rather than working backward from possible callers first. Mark the declarations near refpaths separately; then follow only one hop of direct dependencies. When you encounter a failure branch or an event exit point, make it clear whether it is still local handling within the file or an exit after handing off to an adjacent object. If a thread breaks at a dependency boundary, retain that break as a finding from your reading rather than using the filename to fill it out into a complete chain.

This approach adds a stopping point compared with the early notes. The stopping point does not mean the path relationship ends there; it means this page's responsibility ends there: it records the objects near the GitRefManager entry point that already need to be kept separate. Further material about callers should be covered on the respective pages; repeatedly copying distant relationships here would instead obscure the boundaries within the file.

Sometimes the same code-reading session starts from the mergeTree side. DOC-03 contains side notes on the mergeTree utility functions and can serve as another search signpost; do not merge the objects in it directly back into GitRefManager. Earlier verbal summaries treated the two pages as a single "path utilities area", a classification that has since been withdrawn. They may be adjacent during code reading, but that does not mean they share the same file-level responsibilities.

## Traces of the Past Still on This Page

This page is legacy entry-point material and should not be treated as current interface documentation. It preserves two historical layers: the initial judgment equating the file with the handling location, and the later correction changing the reading order to "declarations—direct dependencies—exit points". Keeping both layers present helps explain why the old links are still valid, while reminding those revisiting the code not to reuse the first layer's conclusion.

The details that have not yet been compiled are quite specific: the names of each direct dependency within the file, the form of the path value at each hop, and the caller-visible behavior corresponding to each failure or event exit point have not been written down here. Someone once wanted to fill in all these details at once; that would have turned a page of entry-point notes into another call-chain description, and the work was not pursued further.

Only one conclusion is retained for now: `src/managers/GitRefManager.js` is the starting point for examining the local relationships around refpaths; when reading, declarations within the file, direct dependencies, and failure/event exit points must be recorded separately. # Symlink Working Tree Entry Decision Record

The old record traced the working-tree issue description all the way to `src/models/GitWalkerFs.js`; initially, it left only a search entry point. The nearby appearance of walker, blob, mode, content, and link here lets reviewers return to the same implementation section, but the issue name alone cannot be used to draw a conclusion for the caller. The later disagreement was not about the link text itself, but about whether the link itself and the object it points to should count as the same working-tree entry.

The IGT-201 reference retains this object terminology, so those still investigating the old repository state can record the rule-file location and findings list. The card preserves the investigation entry point; this record preserves the trade-offs made at the time. Mixing the two would make the findings list look like a behavior definition and make the behavior definition depend on a particular repository layout.

## Scope Defined This Time

This record only constrains the walker's interpretation of working-tree entries. It does not specify whether the caller displays, opens, or parses the target separately after receiving the content, nor does it use whether the target exists as a basis for classifying the entry. The earlier reading—"if the target looks like a directory, continue following it"—has been withdrawn; that puts downstream consumption behavior back into the traversal layer.

Another option was to retain link as a special directory edge and let downstream decide whether to expand it. This would give the caller one fewer branch, but the traversal result for the same entry would vary with the target environment, and the meanings of mode and content would be split across layers. This option was not adopted.

## Decision Made

The working-tree walker returns symlinks as blobs, with mode 120000, content set to the link target, and does not follow descendant entries under the link.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Entry
    Entry --> Blob : Symlink
    Blob --> Mode
    Blob --> Target
    Target --> NoDescendants
    state Entry as "Working-tree entry"
    state Blob as "blob"
    state Mode as "mode 120000"
    state Target as "content is the link target"
    state NoDescendants as "Does not follow descendant entries under the link"
```

This decision fixes the entry boundary at the symlink itself. During review, both mode and content should be recorded; any later intent to read the target belongs to the caller and cannot retroactively change the entry category already returned by the walker. With this handling, the working-tree list can describe links that actually exist in the repository without first determining whether the link target can be traversed further on the current machine.

The specific call sites still need to confirm which consumers only store content and which will treat it as input to a subsequent operation. This question does not affect the decision here, but it will affect whether the caller needs its own path checks. The discussion of absolute gitdir is stored separately at DOC-13, and is not combined with this entry's return semantics.

# Absolute gitdir Discovery Interface Proposal

When the discovery entry point encounters an absolute target, the discussion so far provides insufficient grounds to treat it as a routine path-normalization issue. The review is currently focused on `src/utils/discoverGitdir.js`: first check whether the value returned by this entry point still lets consumers identify the target in the gitdir file, then discuss whether consumers need a different path form.

There were initially two possible approaches.

- Convert the absolute target to a relative path during discovery. The benefit is that subsequent path operations appear to handle only one form; the cost is that the result must depend on a base location for interpretation. If that location is not specified, the meaning of the returned value is unstable.
- Preserve the target text as read during discovery, and leave relative-path calculation to the side that actually needs to use it. This leaves some consumers with one more decision to make, but does not have the discovery entry point choose a reference point for them.

The initial draft favored the first approach only because the relative form is easier to use in subsequent path joins, not because any existing caller had requested it. This preference needs to be reviewed against counterexamples: if the same absolute target yields different text in different working directories, that shows the conversion during discovery has introduced the environment into the result, so "uniform output" can no longer be treated as sufficient justification.

The status returned by the tool must also be preserved separately. Path text and status are not the same thing: the target still being visible does not show that the status has not been lost; the ability to pass the status through does not show that the target has not been processed. During trials, record the two separately rather than using either to vouch for the other.

This round will not change consumers or attempt to extend the scope to trees, worktrees, or other file paths. If preserving the target as read would prevent existing consumers from obtaining the necessary status, stop at the discovery entry point first and clarify the basis it needs for interpretation. If early conversion makes it impossible to refer back to the target as written in the file, withdraw the "convert everything to relative paths" approach.

Still to document: whether any legacy consumers already depend on the form in which absolute targets are returned; which side should specify the reference point for relative paths; where the status returned by the tool is currently passed further up.

# Absolute gitdir Discovery Interface Proposal

The earliest proposal described handling an absolute gitdir as "normalizing it into a more usable form." This wording later proved imprecise, but it is retained: it captures exactly why conversion was moved into the discovery entry point at the time. The recheck still starts at `src/utils/discoverGitdir.js`, but this path serves only as the verification entry point for an absolute gitdir; it does not thereby prescribe path semantics for every consumer.

## Assumptions Left by the Initial Draft

The approach in the year 2023 was: after discovering an absolute target, produce a relative form first so downstream consumers would not have to deal with different representations. The appeal was that call sites would appear to have one fewer branch. It did not answer two earlier questions: what exactly is written in the gitdir file, and which consumer has the authority to decide what "relative" is relative to.

The initial draft conflated these two questions. At the time, a conversion was considered good enough if it remained usable in the current working directory. Later it became clear that "still usable" does not mean the returned value still represents the target written in the file. Once conversion depends on the interpretation location, the result is no longer just the text read from the file.

A rollback condition was also recorded: if the original target cannot be recognized after processing, do not merge. This condition remains, but it only blocks irreversible rewriting; it does not automatically determine which kind of object the discovery entry point should return. Keeping it prevents the next discussion from again skipping the interface meaning on the grounds that the result is "tidier."

## Review Notes

The review did not directly prohibit relative paths; it split "path" in the proposal into three things: the target text in the file, the value the discovery entry point hands to the upper layer, and the interpretation result a consumer obtains in its own context.

That distinction changes where the discussion lands. The discovery entry point can read the target and carry along the tool's existing return status; a consumer that needs a relative form should state which directory it uses as the basis for computing it. If both actions are put into discovery, it becomes difficult for the caller to tell whether the value it receives is file content or a computed result that already includes the environment.

The review also noted that tool-return status must not be treated as an incidental detail. Unchanged path text does not imply that the status is complete; the status still being present does not imply that the target text is unchanged. Each trial from here on should inspect these two separately. No new return object is being designed here on that basis, and there is no assumption that the two must appear in a fixed structure; the existing material supports only the conclusion that they should not substitute for each other.

## Counterexample from the Recheck

The most useful counterexample from the recheck was not a failed path computation, but that once the same absolute target is rewritten into relative form during discovery, the output includes the interpretation location used during discovery. Another consumer may need a different relative result even when looking at the same gitdir file.

This does not mean relative paths cannot be used. A place that genuinely needs a relative form can still compute it; the problem is that when the computation happens too early, the target originally written in the file and the target computed later are collapsed into the same value. What the caller loses is the opportunity to distinguish these two kinds of information.

Someone proposed that, since downstream can always derive the path again, it would be harmless for the discovery entry point to normalize it first. That argument was not carried forward as a proposal. Whether recovery is possible depends on what information remains afterward, and the discovery stage is precisely where it is decided whether the original text is overwritten first. Assigning responsibility for recovery to each consumer also does not establish who should preserve tool-return status.

## Deprecated Wording

Below, the old draft's intent is retained; it is no longer an implementation basis:

> Convert all absolute targets to relative paths, have the discovery layer output only one form, and no longer require callers to decide.

The gap in this passage is not just "uniformity." A relative form always needs a reference, and the draft did not say where that reference came from; "callers no longer need to decide" also hides in the discovery stage the interpretive choice that should have been made by the consumer. The old paragraph is retained because later discussions can easily produce the same variant: convert first and deal with the other questions later.

A more suitable alternative is not to immediately require every consumer to switch to a new object, but to first narrow discovery's responsibilities to the target in the file and the existing status. When a consumer genuinely needs a relative path, it should state why it needs one, what it should be computed relative to, and whether it must revisit the original text after conversion.

## Directions Still Being Compared

**Direction A: Convert during discovery.** This retains the early convenience, but the returned text is affected by the discovery environment, and the caller cannot tell from the result whether conversion has already occurred. It is no longer the default direction.

**Direction B: Preserve the target text at discovery.** This lets the caller—Fang Ke—decide when to interpret it in its own context, at the cost of not being able to assume that all inputs have already been converted to relative form. This direction matches the recheck results, but the scope of existing consumers' dependencies has not yet been listed.

**Direction C: Add a separate interpretation layer.** It could clearly separate reading from computation, but there is not enough material yet to specify the parameters, adopters, or migration order. Keep it as a candidate; do not use this trial to drive implementation.

The trial scope remains limited to the target text, relative path, and tool-return status of an absolute gitdir after it passes through the current discovery entry point. Do not use this to rewrite the tree, checkout paths, or other path rules as well. If preserving the target text leaves an existing consumer without the required status, pause Direction B and first fill in the result for that consumer; if conversion during discovery makes the original text unrecognizable, do not continue with Direction A.

Three questions remain unanswered: which consumers genuinely need the relative form rather than merely being accustomed to receiving it; whether the status can be independently verified when the path text is unchanged; and, if an interpretation layer is added later, how existing consumers should adopt it in batches. This page is still a trial proposal, not a complete public interface specification.

# Absolute gitdir Discovery Interface Proposal

This page was initially placed alongside the discussion of absolute gitdir and was originally intended to answer only a narrow question: after the discovery entry point reads an absolute target, should it also convert it to a relative path for convenience. Later, it was used to revisit `src/utils/discoverGitdir.js`, and also as a record of why the old proposal was not extended further. As a result, the page retains several layers of text that are not entirely consistent: an early judgment about convenience, distinctions between objects made during review, a recheck that was not generalized into a migration conclusion, and a card entry point added only later.

This page should not be read as a general rule for all path objects. It discusses who retains and who interprets the original target text, relative paths, and the tool's return status after a target from a gitdir file enters the discovery process. The edge cases for tree names, checkout paths, and worktree entries still belong in the adjacent material; DOC-14 can serve as navigation, but do not supply conclusions about those objects on behalf of this proposal.

## Initial Notes: Taking "Ease of Use" as the Direction

The earliest draft was short, and its focus was straightforward: if absolute targets were first converted to relative paths, subsequent code would seemingly need to handle only one form. The aim at the time was not to change the interface, but to reduce branching in callers. The discussion assumed that the discovery entry point was closest to the file read, so it was also best placed to perform this conversion.

This assumption had an unstated premise: all consumers could accept the same relative result. The initial draft did not ask what the relative form was relative to, nor did it ask whether some consumers needed only the target read from the file. As long as the path remained usable in the current scenario, the conversion was considered reasonable.

The two approaches listed at the time still illustrate where the debate began.

- One approach was to convert the absolute target to a relative form during discovery. Callers would receive more consistent text, and subsequent concatenation would appear simpler.
- The other approach was to hand over the target from the file during discovery and let consumers that actually needed path calculations handle them themselves. This would avoid choosing a basis for interpretation on the consumers' behalf, but different consumers might retain different pieces of local logic.

The initial draft favored the first approach. The only reason was that "a uniform form" was easier to explain, not that caller dependencies were already understood, or that a complete return-object design already existed at the time. This earlier judgment should not be retrospectively rewritten as the current position; it reflects a state in which reading and interpretation had not yet been separated.

The initial draft also had a stopping condition: if the original target in the gitdir file could no longer be identified after conversion, do not merge it yet. This stopping condition was later retained. It did not tell us what should ultimately be returned, but it identified a loss that should not be accepted lightly: making paths easier to use at the cost of callers no longer being able to see the text in the file.

## Three Questions Raised During Review

The first review did not require the proposal to be implemented or withdrawn immediately, but left only three short questions:

> What is read?
>
> What is returned?
>
> Who decides what it is relative to?

These three questions later came to be cited more often than the original proposal text. The first points to the target text written in the gitdir file; the second points to the path value passed up by the discovery entry point and the tool's return status; only the third concerns an interpretation made by a particular consumer based on its own working directory. The early draft labeled the second and third things as the same "path", thereby making the choice on the consumer's behalf in advance.

The review's conclusion was not "ban relative paths". Relative paths remain a normal local result for consumers that need them. What the review required was this: if the discovery entry point changes the returned form, it must be possible to clearly explain which location the calculation is based on, and whether the caller can still tell what was originally written in the file. Without these explanations, "unification" merely moves complexity somewhere out of sight.

The same review also elevated the status returned by the tool from a secondary concern. In early drafts, status came after path handling, as though it were something carried along incidentally when conversion was complete. The review held that it could not be treated this way. Being able to look back at the path text does not mean the status is still available; being able to pass along the tool status does not mean the target text has not been rewritten. Since then, this page has recorded them side by side, without misrepresenting that parallel treatment as a requirement to add fields or adopt a fixed object structure.

Someone at the meeting said, "As long as it can still be used, that's enough". This did not become the criterion. A value remaining usable at a particular location only proves that the location provides a usable reference for it; it does not prove that the value still expresses the target in the file, much less justify deciding the interpretation location in advance on behalf of other consumers.

## The Retained Old Proposal

The following paragraph comes from an early draft. Its original meaning is preserved, but it is now deprecated:

> Always normalize absolute targets to relative paths first. The discovery layer outputs a single path form, so callers no longer need to decide.

This wording sounded very clean at the time. It assumed that downstream logic would deal with the same type of input, so the earlier the discovery layer unified the form, the better. The problem is that "relative" is not an attribute without an origin. A relative form needs a reference location; if that reference comes from the environment at discovery time, the output already incorporates an environment-dependent calculation and can no longer be treated as a direct expression of the target in the file.

"Callers no longer need to decide" was another major gap in the old proposal. Some consumers may need the original target, while others may need to calculate a relative path from their own location. The old proposal tried to meet both needs with a single calculation performed in advance, but instead left callers unable to know which kind of information they had received.

This section was not deleted because similar suggestions emerged later: shorten the absolute form first, and add status and provenance later. Keeping the old paragraph together with its deprecation marker makes it clearer than the abstract advice "do not convert too early" exactly where that approach lost its basis. It also reminds subsequent reviews not to mistake different path forms for the same interface object.

## Follow-up Review Record: The Problem Is Not an Error in a Particular Calculation

The follow-up review did not produce a checklist that could cover all callers. What it left was a more fundamental counterexample: if the same absolute target is changed to a relative form during discovery, the returned text carries with it the location used to interpret it at that time. Even if this result remains usable at that location, it cannot be said to still be equivalent to the target in the gitdir file.

This point needs to be kept separate from "successful conversion". A relative-path calculation producing a usable result in one working directory only shows that the directory provided a sufficient reference. It does not prove that another consumer should receive the same form, nor does it prove that the discovery function should perform the same calculation on behalf of all consumers. The counterexample is not an argument against relative paths; it points out that the semantics of the output have already changed.

The follow-up review also raised a recovery idea: since downstream code can calculate it again, having the discovery entry point tidy it up first would cause no actual loss. This direction was not pursued. Whether recovery is possible depends on whether the original text is still retained downstream, whether the consumer knows that a conversion occurred, and whether it still has the same basis for interpretation. The discovery entry point is precisely where it is decided whether this information is overwritten first; shifting responsibility for recovery downstream cannot make the information reappear.

Another idea that was not pursued was to package the "original text read" and the "ready-to-use path" into a convenience value with no indication of provenance. It sought to keep callers from dealing with the absolute form, but at the same time left them unable to distinguish which parts came from the file and which came from interpretation. Because the object's meaning could not be clearly defined, this idea was not developed further into an interface design.

This review therefore tightened only one criterion: if a return value does not let callers distinguish the file target from the conversion result, it cannot be taken forward on the grounds of "a uniform format". It did not declare that all callers had been checked, nor did it require all existing users to migrate. The page still leaves these gaps visible to prevent "the old direction was rejected" from being misread as "the new interface is already fully complete".

## The three observations left at the time

Between the two drafts, the objects that actually needed to be clarified gradually settled into three: the target text in the gitdir file, the path value passed to the upper layer by the discovery entry point, and the tool's return status. Listing the three together was not intended to establish a fixed format, but to prevent any one of them from being substituted for another.

For the target text, it is necessary to confirm whether it can still be referred back to, or whether it has already been overwritten by computations during discovery. For relative paths, it is necessary to confirm who computes them, what they are computed relative to, and whether the original target text is still retained afterward. For the tool's return status, it is necessary to confirm whether it is discarded or obscured during path normalization, or merely assumed to exist based on the path text alone.

None of the three can substitute for another. The presence of a status does not prove that the target has not been rewritten; a usable relative form does not prove that the file target is still present; retaining the target text does not mean that the status has been passed through in full. This distinction is the part of this page's trial records that most needs to be preserved over time, because the early debate became ambiguous precisely by collapsing them into a single "path result".

The scope of this page has also remained very narrow: it only examines the behavior of an absolute gitdir after it passes through the current discovery entry point. No material supports extrapolating this to uniform handling of all file paths, much less using it to revise other rules for trees, checkout paths, or working trees. Related issues may also involve paths, but the objects differ, so conclusions cannot be merged merely because the wording is similar.

## Navigation entry point added in 2025

IGT-202 later became a navigation point for this topic. The card requires an absolute gitdir to pass through the discovery entry point in the current file, while retaining both the relative path and the tool's return status. The card continued to use the search notation `absolute gitdir`, so when issues of this kind need to be reviewed, this entry point can be used to return to this page and then distinguish between the early proposals, the review counterexamples, and the later guidance.

This card was not retroactively added to the early versions. Neither the initial draft from 2023 nor the supplementary notes from 2024 included this card, and we should not pretend that the trials were already organized around it at the time. It adds a local entry point for later verification, rather than fabricating completed caller-side results for the early discussions.

The card's phrase "preserve relative paths and the tool's return status" describes what to examine during review, not permission for the discovery entry point to rewrite the target in the gitdir file for that purpose. A relative path may be a local result needed by a particular consumer; the tool status should also be independently reviewable; but neither of these can, in turn, authorize discarding the original text up front during discovery.

The design comparisons and steps taken to begin work recorded on the card show that this issue has reentered the work queue. They do not, on their own, constitute an interface decision, nor do they list the dependencies of legacy consumers. This page therefore remains a trial proposal: it can be used to identify trade-offs and stopping points, but not to declare the migration complete.

## Subsequent Correction

A previous verbal summary was: "An absolute target can first be converted to a relative target, as long as the status is still there." That statement no longer applies. The tool's return status can preserve information about another aspect of the discovery process, but it cannot make up for the target text having already been interpreted prematurely; conversely, preserving the original target text cannot replace passing along the status.

After the correction, the discussion no longer centers on "whether the output is uniform", but instead on deciding whether the discovery layer should preserve the target it reads from the gitdir file. This change does not require every consumer to handle more path logic immediately. It requires the party that actually needs interpretation to explicitly state its own reference point and purpose, rather than letting the discovery entry point choose a location for everyone just because some consumers prefer a relative form.

The phrase "all consumers" in the old draft is therefore no longer valid. The existing material only shows that there are different information needs: some may need to look back at the target in the file, some may need to use relative paths in a local environment, and others need to view the tool's return status as well. Nothing in the material supports collapsing these into a single convenience value with no provenance.

The correction here covers only the discovery stage for absolute gitdir. It does not set rules for other path objects, nor does it claim that all existing callers have already been updated. If a particular consumer has a clear local need, it can still compute a relative path within its own boundary; that computation should make clear which location it uses as its reference, rather than relying on text that has already been silently rewritten during discovery.

## Current Trial Approach

After the old proposal was retained, the objects were separated during review, counterexamples were reviewed, and the card was integrated, the current requirement is stated here: discoverGitdir must preserve the original text of the absolute gitdir target when it encounters an absolute gitdir file, without rewriting it as a relative path.

This requirement only constrains how target text is handled during discovery. The tool's return status should still be reviewable as part of this discovery; consumers that need relative paths compute them in their own contexts. The cost is that some consumers can no longer assume that what they receive is always in relative form, while the benefit is that they can still distinguish the target written in the file from the result they compute themselves.

The current approach does not promise a new interpretation interface, nor does it declare that all legacy callers have completed migration. A dedicated interpretation layer remains a candidate for comparison: it might separate reading from path computation more clearly, but the existing records do not specify its parameters, adopters, or migration order. Presenting a candidate as a settled refactoring would go beyond the available material.

The withdrawal conditions are also more specific than in the initial draft. If preserving the original text would prevent the tool's return status from continuing to be passed along, or if it is later confirmed that a consumer can obtain the necessary basis for interpretation only through the discovery entry point, pause the current direction and first supply the specific result that consumer needs. The fact that relative forms are easier to concatenate is not, on its own, a reason to reinstate the old draft.

## Adjacent Issues Not Yet Split Out

There is still no conclusion on exactly how the status returned by the tool and the path text should be delivered together to consumers. The existing material only establishes that neither should be swallowed up by the other, not whether a new object or additional fields are needed, or whether the existing way of passing them should be retained. For now, this question does not change the requirement to preserve the original text, but it does affect whether consumers can inspect both the target and the status.

If anyone later proposes wrapping the return value, they should first explain which existing information it preserves and how consumers can distinguish the file target from the interpretation result. Simply writing "easier to use" is not enough to answer this question. There is currently no separate migration plan for this issue, nor is there any reason to use this page to expand its scope into changes to all path interfaces.

Another unanswered question is the extent to which existing consumers depend on the relative form. There are not enough caller results here to compile a migration list. IGT-202 is the current navigation entry point, not a dependency list; it helps locate the review context, but does not establish an adoption order on behalf of any consumer.

## Excerpts from review side notes

Two comments written alongside the old review are retained here, and although their tone is not very formal, they are closer to the starting point of the debate than the summaries compiled later:

> Don't call the value you read and the value you intend to use the same "path".
>
> Being able to keep using it does not mean you can still see what was written in the file.

The first comment led to the separation of reading, returning, and interpreting. The second stopped the judgment that "it is enough if the conversion reports no errors" from being applied more broadly. They are not a complete interface manual, nor do they cover other objects; they are retained here to explain why the old draft was not simply renamed and adopted again.

There is also a reminder from a later review: the status and the target text each have value for review. Early discussions tried to prove that the result was complete on the grounds that the status was still present, but that claim has since been corrected. When encountering records that show only one of these in the future, first check whether the other is still visible, rather than inferring the entire discovery process from a single result.

## Old examples appendix

**Old example A: Absolute targets should first be reduced to relative targets.**

This originated as a preference in 2023 and has since been abandoned. It ignores the reference location for the relative form and also inserts the consumer's own interpretation into the discovery stage prematurely. This example is retained to help identify similar proposals, not to guide new implementations.

**Old example B: The presence of the status means the discovery result is complete.**

This claim is also outdated. The status returned by the tool and the target text are independent aspects to inspect; the presence of either cannot automatically prove that the other remains unchanged. If a subsequent review shows only the status, that is not enough to establish whether the target has been rewritten.

**Old example C: A single convenience value can replace both the original text and a usable path.**

This idea did not lead to an implementation plan. The problem with it is not the wrapping itself, but the lack of an explanation of where the value comes from and whether callers can recognize the interpretation that has already taken place. If it is proposed again in the future, the issues exposed by old example A and old example B should be addressed first, and reducing caller-side branching cannot be the only justification.

## Choices when continuing the trial

If the trial continues, first confirm whether the text in the gitdir file can still be viewed again after an absolute target passes through the discovery entry point, and inspect the relative path and the status returned by the tool separately. When a relative form is needed, perform the calculation on the side of the consumer requesting it, and clearly document the basis that consumer uses for interpretation.

There are still only three approaches to compare: early conversion at the discovery entry point, local conversion by the consumer, or a separate interpretation layer. The first remains on record as a rejected historical proposal; the second aligns with the current position; the third still lacks sufficient material to proceed to implementation. These three must not again be merged into a single generalized path cleanup.

This page continues to be cited, because the old draft, corrections made during review, counterexamples from rechecks and the current requirements are still kept in the same place. IGT-202 provide starting points for checking back; this record preserves why the "unified output" approach was not pursued further, and which questions must still be answered clearly first in the next comparison.

# Windows path boundary troubleshooting tree

Start with the path string passed in when checkout or writing fails. Early records split these issues into two cases: Windows drive letters, backslashes, and directory separators mixed together; and names in the repository tree ending up outside the expected directory after concatenation. At the time, the two cases were often grouped together for troubleshooting.

## Investigation order

During review, keep the names seen in the tree, the components before joining, the candidate path after joining, and the directories traversed before writing actually starts. Looking only at the last exception line can easily conflate name validation, path normalization, and link protection into a single issue.

## Old notes from 2023

The original triage rule was: first standardize the separators to match the conventions of the current environment, then decide whether the path is safe. That rule only addressed log readability; it did not say whether the adjusted value could still be used as a repository path. Another old judgment was that all tree names containing colons should be blocked. There was no minimal example to support that judgment at the time; it remains here, but is not being treated as a troubleshooting finding.

## What to check during review

- Is the input an absolute path, or is it made up of directory components? Record the drive letter, root directory, and relative portion separately.
- Do the components include the current directory, parent directory, or internal metadata directory, or do they only have hard-to-see differences such as trailing spaces or dots?
- Does the order of the components change after normalization? If it does, stop; do not continue overwriting the working tree with the normalized string.
- Are any parent directories of the candidate write location symbolic links? Keep the original link target value; do not traverse the link as if it were an ordinary directory.

During one review, directly replacing backslashes made the displayed results look consistent, but did not answer whether tree names and checkout destinations were the same kind of input. That step was later changed from "fix the input" to "save the original value and compare the results." If all you have is the error line, stop the investigation here; without the original components, do not close the path issue.

```text
Failure output
├─ Path form unclear ──> Keep the original input; add a minimal directory tree
├─ Name already rejected in the tree ──> Record the flagged name and rejection point
└─ Target content changed after writing ──> First check whether the parent directory path passes through a link
```

Two questions were still unresolved at the time: whether names containing colons needed platform-specific handling, and whether the write layer or the caller should prove that link targets remain unchanged. # Windows Path Boundary Troubleshooting Tree

When "the path looks normalized, but the result is still rejected" occurs during checkout, first break down the incident context. Preserve the original names in the tree, the components passed in by the caller, the normalized candidate values and the actual write locations; do not overwrite any of these four sets of evidence with another. If the symptom occurs after a write, also preserve the file that was written, the types of the leading directories and the link target. If you have only the last line of the exception and none of these inputs, stop troubleshooting at incident evidence collection, and do not treat the displayed absolute path as a tree name.

## 2023-07: The Initial Directory Rule

The earliest surviving version contained only one narrow working rule: first standardize the separators in Windows paths, then join the resulting string with the repository root. The person recording it was concerned that paths looked different when printed in different terminals, and believed that consistent printed output would allow the subsequent directory checks to be reused. This reasoning did not account for where tree names came from, nor did it distinguish checkout destinations from ordinary filenames.

That page also said: when you see a dot, a parent directory or an internal directory name, delete it from the temporary directory first and then retry. This action was later considered too risky, because it changed the reproduction environment, and could not establish whether rejection occurred during name validation, path joining or at the write entry point. The original statement has not been deleted, and appears in the old appendix at the end; do not follow it in current troubleshooting.

## 2024-01: On-Call Margin Notes

When the same kind of failure occurs on call, ask three questions first: whether the input is a complete path or a set of components passed in individually; whether the failure occurs when the tree is read or just before the destination is created; whether a leading directory may already have been resolved as a link. If the answers are incomplete, only print and compare, without creating directories or deleting files.

The margin notes at the time put "unsafe name" and "destination outside the working tree" in the same column. This made on-call handoffs easier, but left a misconception: as long as the final string was under the root directory, writing could continue. Later tests showed that the location indicated by a path string and the types of directories it traverses cannot substitute for one another. This old margin note is still retained, because many older records reused its columns.

## 2024-06: Disagreements from the First Review

The review used a very small directory tree, not a complete repository. Only one component was changed at a time, with the following recorded: the original component order, the joined path, the rejection point and whether any directories had been created. The tests showed that directly replacing backslashes with slashes only made the output easier to compare, and could not serve as a security check; excluding all names containing colons in advance did not produce a consistent boundary either.

A contrary operational recommendation once appeared here: to avoid platform differences, first convert all tree names into a form accepted by the current system, then enter the checkout flow. This recommendation remains in the review record, but is marked "deprecated". It changes the names being checked, and cannot establish whether the original tree names should be accepted.

If the review results show only the candidate path without listing the component order, stop at "insufficient input evidence". If rejection occurs but it is impossible to identify whether it concerns a tree name or a checkout path, stop at the match list, without continuing to guess at call relationships. The lookup entry point for the path-handling file is `src/utils/resolveFilepath.js`; it provides only local navigation, and cannot supply the missing inputs from the incident.

## 2025-09: Card Samples and Old Images

The minimal directory-tree sample in IGT-203 is used to check Windows path normalization. The public search string on the card is `C:/repo/src/file.txt`, and that string should be used to find records during review. Work began in month 9 on day 10; it was marked blocked in month 9 on day 17, with the recorded reason that the required old-version image had already been cleaned up. When the image is missing, do not replace the old sample with new results, and do not interpret "no image" as a failure of the path rules.

The discovery workflow for IGT-204 starts at the repository root, and retains the final match list. Release classification was done first in month 9 on day 22, and work did not begin until month 9 on day 25. This sequence shows that it is not the same incident entry point as the minimal path sample. If the list contains only issue names without the tree names or checkout destinations that actually matched, stop at list collection first. The search name for the error object is `UnsafeFilepathError`, and records must not be rewritten based on similar exception names.

IGT-205 covers the sample for protection against writes through leading links. A sample was attached in month 9 on day 25, and it was marked blocked in month 9 on day 29, because the previous night's job had expired and the logs could not be retrieved for the time being. When logs are unavailable, inspection may stop at the link itself, the target file and the path before the write; this cannot establish that the protection has taken effect or failed.

These three cards serve only as local entry points. Although tree-name rejection, Windows path joining and writes through links appear under the same exception boundary, troubleshooting must still branch according to the actual symptoms. Directory Filtering Component Boundaries also has DOC-15, so go there when you reach that layer, rather than copying the filtering rules again here.

## Incident Troubleshooting Tree

```text
Symptoms
├─ The joined path differs from the expected directory
│  ├─ Original components are available ──> Preserve their order component by component, then inspect the normalization result
│  └─ Only the final string is available ──> Stop, and obtain the minimal directory tree and input records
├─ A tree name or checkout destination is rejected
│  ├─ The specific component can be identified ──> Preserve the match list and error object
│  └─ Only the call failure is known ──> Do not rename anything or replace separators, and return to the discovery entry point
└─ The link target changes after a write
   ├─ Leading components are visible ──> Preserve the link and target, and stop further writes
   └─ Leading components are not visible ──> Stop at incident evidence collection, and wait for path records that can be reviewed
```

## 2025-11: Current Verification Criteria

The operational boundaries for the current version begin here, while the earlier rules remain in their original historical context. Verification starts by breaking down the inputs, then checks for name rejection, and finally checks the leading components before writing. If original evidence is missing at any of these three steps, report only the gap, without substituting speculation for results.

Windows path join normalizes C:\repo, src, file.txt to C:/repo/src/file.txt, while preserving the component order.

Validation of tree names and checkout destination rejects .,..,.git and aliases involving case differences or trailing characters and throws UnsafeFilepathError; ordinary foo:bar names remain valid.

Any write must be rejected if a leading component is a symbolic link, and the target file pointed to by the link must remain unchanged.

Actual troubleshooting therefore has three stopping points. First, if the joined result is inconsistent with the component order, stop at path joining, without proceeding to name validation. Second, when the rejection boundary is hit, preserve the rejected tree name or checkout destination and the error object, without replacing it with the broader label "invalid path". Third, when the write path passes through a symbolic link, stop at the write entry point, and confirm that the target file pointed to by the link has not been changed before addressing subsequent issues. When an ordinary `foo:bar` reaches name validation, it must not be sent directly to the rejection branch merely because it contains a colon.

The minimum verification evidence in order is: the original input, the component list, the normalization result, the matched component, the leading directories before the write, the link target and the failure output. It is not always possible to obtain all the evidence; when something is unavailable, stop at the corresponding branch.`C:/repo/src/file.txt` describes only one searchable path sample, and does not replace the actual inputs from the incident. Use `UnsafeFilepathError` only when that error object is actually present, rather than applying this name to all ordinary failures.

## Review Excerpts and Follow-Up Referrals

During review, someone proposed combining the three failures into a single "path exception" state, on the grounds that the on-call interface needed only one entry point. This opinion is retained, but was not adopted: a combined state would lose the component order and leading-link information, and these two pieces of information determine whether the next step can still be retried safely. The final approach retained navigation on the same page with three local branches.

Another suggestion was to make the caller responsible for resolving symbolic links first, then passing the real directory to the write layer. This proposal was not included in the current criteria, because it would change path semantics before the protection is applied. The follow-up work to confirm whether the caller has already preserved the original components remains unresolved; it belongs to integration testing with the caller, and no conclusion is added on this page.

When looking back through the cards, IGT-203 is suitable for checking the minimal Windows directory tree, IGT-204 is suitable for checking the rejection match list, and IGT-205 is suitable for checking the sample involving writes through leading links. Status changes on the cards do not replace the judgments on this page; in particular, the cleanup of old images and job expiration only explain why evidence was missing at the time.

## The Old Appendix Still Retained

> Old procedure: first replace all path separators with the current system's convention, then continue checkout. If it still fails, delete the temporary directory and retry.
>
> ——This is a verbatim excerpt from an early working context and is deprecated. It overwrites the original components, and also destroys the conditions needed to reproduce writes through links. Do not treat it as a current procedure.

> Old classification: temporarily treat names containing colons as dangerous names.
>
> ——A later review found this classification too broad, and it has been replaced by the current name boundary; the appendix has not been deleted, as it may still be used to search old reports.

An adjacent issue also remains here: some error output provides only the final target path, without saying whether it comes from joining tree names or is a checkout destination. This issue has not yet been split into a separate entry point. When encountering such output, preserve the original text and call context, stop at input breakdown, and do not attribute the cause based on the path's appearance.

IGT-206 moved from To Do to In Progress at 2025-09-15T12:13:52+08:00. The card requires verifying "Directory Filtering Component Boundaries" with the repository's own path checks and recording one hit and one miss. By 2025-09-22T15:13:52+08:00, the card had moved to Blocked, with the reason "Worktree Traversal's test machine is tied up with other regression runs today." During verification, start with the local declarations and adjacency relationships indicated by the old entry point. Record the objects observed, the call sites, and the path conditions separately. If you can only see a traversal entry point, not the component traversed by the filtering check, stop at recording the entry point and do not infer anything downstream. Matching directory names, similar names, or all having walker in the name are not grounds for inclusion.

Save the results in two columns:

| Record | What to retain | Conclusions that cannot be drawn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hit | Input path, component traversed, call site | Adjacent calls outside this component automatically belong in this batch |
| Miss | Similar path, the fact that it did not pass through this component, time of the recheck | The filtering component does not exist, or this path will never be relevant |

A hit record only places an object in the candidate set; you still need to confirm that the caller is actually within the directory filtering boundary. Miss records are retained to prevent later expansion of the scope based on a single successful sample. If either type of record is missing, the target component still should not be added to the migration table.

Once the target path has been confirmed by checking references within the current revision, handle callers that fall directly within the filtering boundary first, then look at adjacent calls. Adjacent calls must have hit records showing that they pass through the same component; merely sharing `src`, `model`, or a directory level is not enough.

At this stage, each migration batch only needs to record the old path, target path, and hit conditions. Keep the old path in place until the batch is complete so callers exhibiting problems can be put back on the original entry point. If the target has not yet been confirmed, do not create a batch based on assumptions or treat the entire file as a replaceable unit.

If a rollback is needed, first restore the old references for the callers in this batch and retain both the hit and miss records. Do not change the path conditions while restoring the path; if both variables change together, it will be impossible later to tell whether the wrong component was selected or the input classification had changed.

To add: the target component, direct callers, reasons for excluding adjacent calls, and the minimal set of paths to recheck after restoring the old path.

# Directory Filtering Component Boundary Migration Guide

The entry point left by the earlier investigation is still `src/models/GitWalkerRepo.js`. It is where the issue name and call name led, and is useful for taking people back to the earliest verification point; it is not the name of the directory filtering component, nor is it a migration target that can be used as a direct replacement. The fact that directory traversal, path filtering, and callers appear near the same starting point for rechecking does not mean they fall within the same component boundary.

Use this page in the order of the old entry point, boundary verification, updating references in batches, and restoring the old paths. The actual objects still need to be confirmed through local declarations and reference relationships within the frozen scope of `internal/iso-core`, `v_prev`. If no target has been confirmed, it is better to leave fields blank than to include `GitWalkerRepo` or its containing directory wholesale.

```text
Earlier investigation records
    |
    v
src/models/GitWalkerRepo.js
    |
    +-- Path check hit ----> Candidate filtering component + call site
    |
    +-- Similar path miss --> Retain as an exclusion record
    |
    v
Update references in batches by caller after target confirmation
    |
    +-- Unexpected result: restore the old references for this batch
```

## Why the Entry Point Is Retained

The earliest records contained only the issue name, call name, and a few words from file paths: `walker`, `src`, `model`, `models`. These clues explain why the investigation started at `src/models/GitWalkerRepo.js` at the time, but they cannot tell us which object makes the filtering decision. The first version left the target component, compatible callers, and hit conditions blank, and these blanks were part of the information state at the time and should not be filled in in later versions to create a seemingly complete mapping.

The old entry point also has a role during migration. If a recheck produces different results, you can return to the same file and compare the new reference relationships with the existing path records; if callers whose references have been updated need to be restored, there is also a most recently recorded location to return to. Here, "retention" only covers the period between verification and batch migration, and does not mean the old entry point will never change, much less that its component assignment has already been confirmed as correct.

If subsequent checks confirm that the filtering logic is not in this file, the old path is still retained as a historical entry point until the relevant batches are complete. Deleting it too early would leave people relying only on the filename to recall what was previously checked, without being able to distinguish the traversal entry point indicated by the old records from the newly confirmed filtering component.

## Constraints Left by the Second Recheck

Work on IGT-206 began at 2025-09-15T12:13:52+08:00, with a requirement to use the repository's own path checks to verify "Directory Filtering Component Boundaries" and retain one hit and one miss. The focus of this requirement is the component that the input actually passes through, not whether a directory name sounds like filtering logic, and not including the entire surrounding area in scope just because a walker-related object is found.

At 2025-09-22T15:13:52+08:00, the card moved from In Progress to Blocked, with the reason "Worktree Traversal's test machine is tied up with other regression tests today". This status record only explains why that recheck was interrupted. It does not identify the object hit, does not provide a target path, and does not provide a list of compatible callers. Therefore, the second version can only establish the checking method and record fields, and cannot claim that the boundary has been determined.

The test machine being occupied does not change component assignment. When the machine becomes available again, local declarations and adjacency relationships must still be examined starting from the old entry point, and the hits and misses from the path checks must then be recorded separately. A check that was not run is not a miss; an empty result cannot substitute for the other type of record either.

An early working assumption was: since the issue name points to `GitWalkerRepo`, the filtering boundary is here. This statement is retained as the starting point at the time, but it no longer applies. What the later recheck withdrew was not the old entry point itself, but the practice of inferring component assignment directly from the entry point's location.

## First Separate the Three Objects During Verification

When rechecking `src/models/GitWalkerRepo.js`, first record the traversal entry point, path conditions, and referenced objects separately. Objects in a file may be adjacent and closely connected by calls, but unless the path filtering decision has been observed passing through a component, that object cannot be listed as a migration target.

The first type of record is entry point information: it answers which file and which local location to continue investigating from. The second is filtering boundary information: it answers whether an input passes through a candidate component. Only the third is caller information: it answers which usage site needs its reference updated. If these three types of content are mixed into a single "file ownership" conclusion, it will no longer be possible to tell whether a given migration changed the entry point, filtering conditions, or callers.

Within the current scope, revision only defines the time boundary for rechecking. Earlier investigation records provide a starting point, but cannot replace reference verification in `v_prev`. If local declarations only show traversal relationships, stop the record there; do not infer filtering relationships from the directory hierarchy, and do not treat similarly named objects as the same boundary.

## Retain Hits and Misses in Pairs

The minimum result of a path check is two comparable records:

| Result | Recorded content | Meaning for migration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hit | Input path, candidate component the input passed through, call site | May be included in a candidate batch, pending caller verification |
| Miss | Similar path, the fact that it did not pass through that component, corresponding recheck location | Retain as grounds for exclusion, do not include in that batch |

A hit does not mean references can be changed immediately. It first establishes that the candidate component is indeed on a particular input path, after which the caller must still be confirmed to be within the directory filtering boundary. A caller merely being in the same directory as the target object, also being in `src/models`, or just sharing a similar name is not sufficient for inclusion.

Nor is a miss proof of the opposite. It may only mean that this one similar path did not take the same branch; it does not mean the component does not exist, nor does it guarantee that all similar paths in the future will avoid that component. Miss records are retained so that subsequent scope checks can see the excluded counterexamples, rather than expanding the scope based solely on hit samples.

If there is only a hit and no miss for a similar path, do not report the boundary as finalized; if there is only a miss, do not abandon the old entry point on that basis either. In both cases, keep the target component blank and add the missing path record. This way, during the next recheck, the missing item is clearly identified, rather than generalized into a vague status of "testing incomplete".

## Migrate in Batches by Caller After Confirmation

The target path can only be established by verifying references in the current revision. After confirmation, handle callers that fall directly within the filtering boundary first, then assess adjacent calls separately. This is not to split up the migration as a formality, but to avoid incorrectly changing a nearby call site simply because it shares a folder or a traversal entry point.

Each batch only needs three items recorded: the original reference location, the confirmed target path, and the hit conditions that support the reference change. Caller changes should be traceable back to the corresponding hit records; there is no need to list unverified callers just to fill out the table. The current materials provide neither a complete caller list nor a confirmed target component, so this page does not specify an exact number of batches.

Changing the direct callers first also has a recovery benefit. If the results differ from expectations, the impact is limited to the current batch, and you can return to the old entry point and compare the two types of path records again. Whether adjacent calls warrant a separate batch depends on whether the hit records show that they pass through the same filtering component, not on whether they are adjacent to the objects in the first batch.

During adaptation, do not change the entry point and filtering conditions at the same time. If both are changed together, unexpected behavior cannot be attributed to either a caller being redirected to the wrong component or a change in the input's path conditions. Until the target boundary is confirmed, callers should continue using the existing access method; this does not establish that the old path is correct, but avoids replacing verification with a compound change.

## Branch for Restoring the Old Path

Only if this batch's target path was changed incorrectly should you first revert the caller references in that batch to the recorded old entry point, then compare the pre-change hits and misses. Do not adjust filtering conditions in passing during restoration, otherwise the restored results will include both path selection and condition changes and will not show which action caused the difference.

If the path conditions have also changed, restore in two steps. First restore the original conditions and confirm that inputs still separate into hits and misses in the original way; then restore the caller paths and confirm that the call sites return to the old entry point that can be rechecked. These two steps cannot be collapsed into a single "restored", because the first and second steps concern different objects.

Restoring the old path does not reconfirm the previous component assignment. It only returns callers to the last entry point with a clear historical record. After restoration, the similar paths that previously missed must still be checked, to avoid expanding the scope again based only on hit samples. If the old and new results identify only the traversal entry point and not the filtering component, stay at the entry point record and do not initiate another reference change.

## Fields Still Blank

Within `internal/iso-core`, this page can currently provide `src/models/GitWalkerRepo.js` as the verification entry point, with `v_prev` as the recheck point in time. IGT-206 provides the specific requirement to retain one hit and one miss, but does not supply a target component that can be entered directly, a complete set of compatible callers, or results showing migration completion.

Therefore, what can currently be done is: starting from the old entry point, record traversal, filtering, and callers separately; retain both types of path results; once the target is confirmed, update references with direct callers taking priority; if unexpected behavior occurs, restore the paths for the current batch first, then handle condition changes separately. The target path, caller list, and minimal recheck path still need to be added to their corresponding batches, and cannot be filled in based on filenames or a blocked status.

Grouping the two under one test at the time saved time finding an entry point, but also blurred the distinction between their assessment criteria.

The later review established only that `__tests__/test-clone-checkout-huge-repo.js` provided navigation around checkout; the record does not show that both write aggregation and file-level restore were fully exercised there. This review kept the original split rather than combining the two questions into a single assertion again:

- For Multiple Write Failure Aggregation, prepare one set of calls with success followed by failure, and another set of successful calls.
