versions.body:
# cherry-pick boundary troubleshooting tree

The old on-call notes have never been removed. It started simply: someone brought several commit-related anomalies into the area around `src/api/commit.js`, and this page then came to be treated as an entry point for handling three things. Those three things were called cherry-pick Shared Result, binary merge Conflict, and symlink cherry-pick Link Boundary. They appeared during the same round of work and were later included in the same set of regression materials; but they were not the same symptom.

The early version mistakenly treated "seeing a commit call" as a sufficient shared premise. That approach made it easy to write quick on-call notes: trace commit and tree in the notes, say the result was already at the API layer if a call returned, say the investigation could continue from the same point if a merge got stuck, and file symlink entries that appeared in the working tree under this page too. That grouping was not split apart at the time, so the old entry point remains at the very beginning of the document. It is useful for finding the initial search location, not for collapsing three situations into a single judgment.

The tree below shows the old workflow, retained to explain why the subsequent observations were overstated at the time. "Continue" in the tree only means continuing to gather observations of the same type of situation; it does not mean the cause has been found.

```text
An anomaly near a commit call?
|
+-- Can you identify what a call actually returned or threw?
|   |
|   +-- Yes → Put it in the cherry-pick Shared Result column first
|   |
|   `-- No → Do not use working-tree changes to fill in its result
|
+-- Is the merge situation described as binary merge Conflict?
|   |
|   +-- Yes → Keep a separate description of the merge situation
|   `-- No → Do not treat a normal return as evidence of a conflict
|
`-- Does the situation point to symlink cherry-pick Link Boundary?
    |
    +-- Both successful and failed calls are available → Record what is visible for each separately
    `-- Only one side is available       → Stop at this branch, do not apply the other branch's conclusion
```

There is a problem here that only became apparent later: the tree places "public result" at the top level, making it look as though the other two branches should both pass through it first. That was not a confirmed API rule, just an ordering chosen by the author of the first draft to shorten troubleshooting time. binary merge Conflict does not become a result branch just because a call returned earlier; nor can a symlink's working-tree entry automatically be matched to the returned content just because someone mentioned cherry-pick during the same round of work. The old version did not spell out this distinction, making it easy for readers at this point to treat one visible output as a common explanation for all three problems.

## The old entry point still starts here

`src/api/commit.js` is the first location retained on this page. The old troubleshooting records point to it through the issue name and call name, and also repeatedly mention commit, tree and commit calls. It can help narrow the scope of reading to the vicinity of commit API, but it cannot replace verification of the specific situation. The early records used it in precisely that latter way: upon seeing similar names, they bundled implementation ownership, call location and exception boundaries into a single judgment.

If you are taking over an old ticket, the first step is simply to confirm which object it refers to. If the question mentions "public result", ask what the call actually returned or threw; do not switch to asking whether the working tree changed. If the question mentions "binary merge Conflict", retain the label "conflict" and ask the module maintainer to verify the current version's behavior and the entry point for further inspection. If the question mentions "symlink cherry-pick Link Boundary", you need the visible contents from one successful call and one failed call respectively. Without material from both sides, this branch should stop.

This does not mean that every situation needs to be written up as a long report. For a public result, the minimum record is a call and what it actually handed to the caller. For binary merge Conflict, the minimum record is the inspection entry point identified by the maintainer. For the symlink boundary, the minimum record is what the successful and failed calls each left behind. The old page once tried to collapse these differences into a single "commit result" field, making it difficult in retrospect to tell whether that field referred to what was returned, what was thrown, the merge situation, or a working tree entry.

## The earlier misjudgment: treating a return as a boundary

The initial draft described cherry-pick Shared Result too directly. The judgment at the time was: as long as the caller saw a result, that result could be treated as the public boundary of cherry-pick; any merge or link anomalies encountered afterward would only require returning to the same commit entry point to continue tracing. This judgment did not distinguish between "what the call actually returned or threw" and "changes visible in the working tree after the call". The two may be mentioned in the same description, but they are not the same record.

There is a shortcut in the old procedure that can still mislead people today: first find a normal return, then use it to explain the failure situation. This is tempting when there are very few records, because a normal call appears to provide a point of reference for a failed call. But for these three objects, that comparison is not automatically valid. A sample of a public result can only show what that call left behind; it cannot fill in the merge situation for binary merge Conflict, nor can it fill in the link boundary on the failure side for symlink.

Therefore, when handling the old text, the following sentence should be treated as historical guidance rather than an actionable conclusion:

> With one normal cherry-pick return, the conflicts and symbolic link anomalies from the same round can initially be grouped under the same public result.

This sentence has been retained because it explains why the old records kept returning to the same code vicinity. It does not provide enough branch conditions. In particular, after "one more location is still unconfirmed" was raised later, using this sentence again to classify things quickly would only hide what remains unknown.

The common-result branch can continue through a narrower sequence: first record whether the caller saw a return or a throw; if neither was recorded, mark only "No call result obtained". If a call result has been recorded, then check whether it is exactly the cherry-pick Shared Result referred to in the question. Do not put tree, checkout paths, or symlink entries into the result field here. They may be accompanying observations from the same incident, but they cannot replace the call content.

If an old ticket only says "the result is wrong" and does not specify whether it was a return, a throw, or a working-tree change, the old version would have readers follow `src/api/commit.js` downward directly. This can serve as a starting point, but first clarify the meaning of the question. Otherwise, any local declaration encountered will be overinterpreted as external behavior. This page does not preserve a result format that unifies the three meanings, nor does it preserve samples proving that they are equivalent.

## Do not borrow return samples for the binary merge Conflict branch

binary merge Conflict took up only a very short section in the old draft, not because it had already been confirmed, but because the original recorder treated it as a failure mode of the common-result branch. This inference was never subsequently substantiated. The available working entry point is still: ask the maintainer of the relevant module to verify how binary merge Conflict behaves in the current version and identify an entry point for further checking.

If the maintainer provides an entry point, record the entry point together with this issue; do not append a generic return from a commit afterward as though it could explain the conflict. If the response you receive is something like "still needs verification", do not rewrite this branch as already recovered. The problem with the old page is precisely that it often wrote "conflict-side material has not yet been obtained" as "there is no conflict". These two statements are not the same: the former describes a gap in the record, while the latter describes behavior.

The old tree described this branch as "merge process stopped → handle as a conflict". The advantage of this wording is that it does not let binary merge Conflict leak into the common-result field; the drawback is that "stopped" does not say who saw what. When retaining this branch, retain the object name from the original question instead of replacing it with "commit failed". "Commit failed" will once again conflate the call return, the merge state, and the working-tree symptoms.

This page contains no fixed signal that can be used to determine that binary merge Conflict has disappeared. The fault-classification action only indicates that this issue was once classified as a failure; it does not mean that the root cause has been established, nor that every subsequent commit call will reproduce it. An earlier version treated failure classification as a sign that "the entry point was locked down"; this level of interpretation is too strong and is retained here only as a note on the old practice.

For records requiring further follow-up, the shortest branch is as follows:

```text
Is the question explicitly about binary merge Conflict?
├─ Yes: ask the module maintainer to verify the current behavior and record the checking entry point they provide
│   ├─ Entry point provided: continue via that entry point; do not use a common-result sample as a substitute
│   └─ Entry point not provided: leave it pending verification; do not judge it to be "recovered"
└─ No: return to the question's original wording and confirm whether it is actually about a return or a symlink boundary
```

This passage does not assign the scope of responsibility to a fixed owner. The old record only offers the hint "maintainer of the corresponding module" and does not provide a more detailed mapping. Expanding this into specific names or ownership of specific implementations would lead later readers to mistakenly believe that a clear conclusion had already been reached at the time.

## The symlink case must include both sides

symlink cherry-pick Link Boundary was once raised as "the output cannot be reproduced consistently". The old page's initial response was to treat it as an unstable shared result: since both were cherry-pick, the result of a normal call could first be used as a reference. This approach did not retain the corresponding content from the failed call, nor did it explain whether the link boundary actually appeared on the successful side or the failed side. It turned "cannot be reproduced consistently" into an overly broad label.

The actionable requirement from the earlier work is somewhat clearer here than in the initial draft: retain the visible results of symlink cherry-pick Link Boundary from one successful call and one failed call separately. Here, "separately" matters. The successful side is not there to prove the failed side wrong, nor is the failed side there to invalidate the successful side; each shows what that call left behind. If there is only one sample, do not fill the gap with "the other side is the same".

The old draft also described "a working-tree entry with a symbolic link in the working tree" as a sufficient condition for pinpointing the issue. This is also too strong a claim. A working-tree entry can prompt an investigator to follow the symlink branch, but it cannot establish the link boundary on its own, nor can it show that this case and binary merge Conflict share the same cause. Even if the two phenomena were recorded around the same time, their evidence should still be kept separate.

The following recording framework can be used to continue work on this branch without broadening its meaning:

| Side | What to retain | What to do if missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Successful call | The visible results of that call | Do not fill in with text from the failed side |
| Failed call | The visible results of that call | Mark as not yet obtained, and do not infer the link state |
| Comparison of both sides | Record only differences that can actually be compared | Do not state a comparison conclusion without both sides |

This table is not a complete verification procedure that already existed in the old version. It merely separates the requirements for the successful and failed sides that had already been raised in the old card, to avoid reverting to the old draft's "one output is enough" wording. As for whether there is a deeper relationship between the link itself, the tree name, and the checkout path, this page contains no material on that. Do not invent such a relationship based on the title.

One simplified approach was: if the symlink behavior does not appear on the second call, treat it as sporadic output. This approach should now be explicitly marked as deprecated. It did not specify what to retain separately for the second call and the first, nor did it address cases where the "successful call" and the "failed call" involved different questions. What it provided was a convenient way to close out the record, not comparable evidence from the case.

## Stopping points between the three branches

The easiest way to misread this page is to treat stopping points as failures. In fact, a stopping point only indicates that the current material cannot support the next classification step. The stopping points listed below apply to the minimum wrap-up needed when preserving the old records:

- We only know that someone mentioned cherry-pick, but do not have what the call actually returned or threw: stop at the public-result sampling point.
- We only know the name of binary merge Conflict, but do not have the current behavior or inspection entry provided by the module maintainer: stop at the conflict-check point.
- We only have one of the symlink's two sides—the success side or the failure side: stop between the records for the two sides; do not make a stability judgment.
- If worktree entries, call returns, and the merge context are written in the same sentence, making their respective sources indistinguishable: split the original sentence first, then continue.

The old version had none of these stopping points. It tended to infer the other two branches from a single observed phenomenon, especially combining the evidence under the guise of a "same-round commit anomaly." That approach can make a card appear to finish faster, but the next time a similar name appears, it leaves no way to know which section should be reused.

Nor should this be turned around into requiring all three branches to be completed in one go. The only thing they have in common is that they are placed in the same Integrity Window 1.0 record, and that all the old entry points start near commit API. The public-result branch already has a question from the caller side; the maintainer needs to provide an entry point for binary merge Conflict; the symlink boundary needs visible content from both the success and failure cases. Their evidence takes different forms, so the troubleshooting order can differ.

## A few later-added traces from the field

By the time this page was revised for the second time, the related work already had several follow-up actions. cherry-pick Shared Result was classified as a failure case, and the card's handling target was later adjusted because the issue fell in another part of the implementation. This adjustment cannot be used to infer that `src/api/commit.js` had been ruled out, nor that the new location was the sole cause; it only shows that the old page framed the troubleshooting entry point too much in terms of implementation ownership.

A brief public addendum was later left: cherry-pick Shared Result still has one unconfirmed point. This status conflicts with the original draft's wording, "an existing return is enough to classify it." The old wording was not deleted because it explains why early records placed the public result first; however, it should no longer be treated as a completion condition.

binary merge Conflict was also classified as a failure case, and a caller walkthrough took place afterward. The walkthrough itself is not a conclusion; it only indicates that someone viewed the relevant path from the caller side. In the old version, when it encountered an action such as "caller walkthrough," it would often write in the body, "the caller has confirmed it"; this rewrite is inaccurate. Here, retain it only as a trace that someone later continued to inspect the entry point.

The symlink branch underwent a risk review; the subsequent public addendum still said, "There is still one unconfirmed point; update it when the next fact arrives." This is exactly why the old page should not be treated as the current stable workflow: it requires visible content from two calls, but does not retain those two pieces of content; it starts with the inability to reproduce reliably, but provides no comparison record that would let the reader assess stability.

These supplementary notes also make clear that none of the three branches has reached an overall conclusion that can replace the original incident context. Putting the three matters on the same page can at most provide a triage order and the sources of past judgments; follow-up actions in any one branch cannot be presented as verification of another.

## The Old Approach Still Retained

The following is a simplified version commonly used during early on-call shifts, deliberately left unchanged rather than updated to the current guidance:

1. When you see descriptions related to cherry-pick, first go back to the area around the commit.
2. When a value is returned, record the result as a common result.
3. Initially group the binary merge Conflict and symlink behavior observed in the same round with that result.
4. If the same output is not seen the second time, provisionally record it as intermittent.

These four steps explain the order of entries in the old documentation, but they set the evidence threshold too low for the different issues. In particular, the third and fourth steps can conceal the lack of a conflict entry point and the lack of call results from the failing side. The old approach was not deleted because historical cards had been read using this classification; deleting it outright would instead remove the background explaining "why the early materials were used interchangeably".

Another approach that was not continued was to first decide that all issues belonged to tree, then infer what happened on the caller side from changes to tree. This also lacks sufficient evidence. In the old entry, tree is merely an adjacent term, and cannot replace call returns, thrown exceptions, the merge context or records from both sides of a symbolic link. Using it as a unified explanation would lead readers to believe that this page already covers the full behavior of commit API, when what actually remains is only a partial working record of these three types of issues.

## Sentences to Take Away at Handoff

If an old card still requires follow-up questions to someone, keep the questions narrow. For the common result, ask: "What did this call actually return or throw?" For binary merge Conflict, ask: "What is the behavior in the current version, and where is the entry point for further investigation?" For symlink, ask: "What did the successful call and the failed call each leave behind?" Keeping the questions narrow can prevent the responder from replying with only "the commit is fine" or "cannot reproduce", but such replies cannot fill the gaps in any of the three branches.

The relevant entry points are at IGT-213, IGT-214 and IGT-215. The three cards serve different purposes: the first retains the unconfirmed items for the public result path, the second points to the current verification entry point for binary merge Conflict, and the third retains the content still to be recorded on the symlink success side, as well as on the failure side. DOC-20 deals with Logs with Changed Lines, and should not be used to interpret the links or merge branches on this page.

The conclusion still follows the old page's conservative approach: do not write a public result when there is no invocation content; do not write that it has been handled when there is no conflict-side entry point; do not write that symlink is stable without both the success and failure sides. This stopping point is narrower than the earlier quick categorization, but it does not invent a common answer for three things that remain unconfirmed.

# Change-Line Log Migration Verification

This page originally was just a lookup record: someone started from the name Logs with Changed Lines, searched near the issue name and call name, and eventually landed on `src/api/log.js`. At that time, what was needed was to find a readable file quickly; no complete page operation was recorded, and file hits, log results, and whether callers could continue using it were not separated. What is being added now is the sequence for migration verification and the provenance of the old record, not a reorganization of this page into a new log interface specification.

## Two routes left on paper

The old record's route was very short. First find `log`, then look at `history` and `commit` near the same place, and then use `path`, `row`, and `mode` to cross-check Logs with Changed Lines. It was suitable for leading someone into the file, but did not explain which action on the page would produce a result. Between the filename, local declarations, and the line seen by the user, the original record linked only the first segment.

The route after the addendum still starts from this entry, but adds a checkpoint in the middle: first lock down the `v_prev` corresponding to the old material, then inspect the references and local declarations under that revision, and only then perform the page action. If another revision is being checked, record the result separately; do not overwrite the old record with the new material. This did not produce a new filename; the so-called new entry point means putting the revision reference and page result into the lookup chain, rather than treating a name hit as the endpoint.

```text
Old record route
Issue name / call name
        |
        v
src/api/log.js @ v_prev
        |
        v
log / history / commit

Supplemental verification route
References to v_prev
        |
        v
Local declarations for src/api/log.js
        |
        v
Logs with Changed Lines: path / row / mode
```

The two routes in this diagram are not two implementations. The upper one preserves the lookup habit actually used by the old page, while the lower one merely reconnects the verification actions that were originally missing. `src/api/log.js` is the file entry that can be retained in the current material; its more distant implementation ownership cannot be assigned based solely on its directory location.

## What the June draft did not answer

The draft contained an implicit assumption: as long as the issue name or call name could lead back to `src/api/log.js`, compatibility migration could continue along this file. That assumption explained at the time why the investigation started from the file, but there was not enough material to prove three things: whether the reference still pointed here, whether the local declaration covered Logs with Changed Lines, and whether `row` and `mode` shown on the page came from the same result.

Therefore, "finding the file" can only count as the first status on this page. It shows that the old index is still useful; it does not mean that the migration is complete. In particular, do not infer all of `history`'s behavior from the name `log`, and do not fill in the meaning of `row` or `mode` merely because `path` appears on the page. The portion containing the actual output was not saved in the old record and is still treated as unconfirmed.

The old draft also wrote the entry, result, and compatibility as several adjacent sentences. They are separated now in order to preserve the historical position of that judgment. People who use this page later may still find the file through the old index; if that passage were directly changed to "confirmed," it would instead erase why the early investigation stopped here.

## Follow one record

First, copy the original clues. Retain the issue name, call name, and the location where they lead someone to `src/api/log.js`. When the search terms are near `commit`, `history`, `log`, `path`, `row`, and `mode`, these terms can be used as clues for checking back, but do not expand matched terms into implementation relationships. Keep clues and evidence in separate columns so it is clear later which items were only entry points.

Second, fix the material version. The old investigation corresponds to `v_prev`. The verifier should first confirm which revision the reference belongs to, and then read the local declarations related to logging in that revision. If the available material does not show where the reference lands, record only "pending confirmation"; do not substitute a matching filename for the reference relationship. If the reference has already changed to another revision, retain the old record and start the new verification from another record.

Third, inspect the object relationships. First look at `log`, `history`, and `commit` that appear directly in the file, and then inspect their adjacency to `path`, `row`, and `mode`. Record the local relationships that are actually observed here; do not automatically include nearby directory contents in the migration scope. The original record supports only this file entry and these object terms; it cannot establish the names of other log pages or callers.

Fifth, discuss compatibility. The page result only explains what this page action left behind; the caller result requires separate material. If the caller has not provided a concrete result, record only through the page review. Do not write it as proof of post-migration compatibility just because the same call name once located the file.

## The old arrangement of migration batches

It was originally suitable to split the work into three batches, but each batch had a different stopping point. The first batch handled objects with existing old investigation records: follow the issue name and call name to the file, save the results showing where they led, and then review the references under the same `v_prev`. The output of the first batch is an entry record, not a page compatibility conclusion. If the file path still cannot be found, retain the old index clues and the gap.

The second batch supplements the page flow. To retain the Logs with Changed Lines result, it must at least be possible to identify `path` and `row` on the page, and copy down `mode` as well. If the page shows only the entry, only partial fields, or a result whose originating action cannot be confirmed, the batch stops at unconfirmed. Without new output, do not rewrite the judgment in the June draft.

Only the third batch deals with callers. The current material has no specific caller name and no new file path that can be cited directly. When a caller provides only an issue name, first return to the old entry and revision; when the caller can provide a page result, attach that result under the object. Results from neighboring projects or similar logs cannot replace the record on this page.

The following note can be used to determine how far the process has progressed:

| Position | What remains at hand | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File entry | Issue name, call name, `src/api/log.js` | Verify the references to `v_prev` |
| Local declarations | `log`, `history`, `commit`, and adjacent fields | Perform the page action |
| Page result | Logs with Changed Lines output | Compare against `path`, `row`, and `mode` |
| Caller result | Result of the specific user flow | Record the compatibility judgment separately |
| Missing material | Only an index hit or verbal description | Stop at unconfirmed |

"File entry" in the table is not an approval marker. It only means that the investigation can start here. A page result also does not automatically include a caller result; this is exactly where the layers in the old draft were too close together.

If the new verification route produces no result, first retain the point at which this failure occurred, then return to the issue-name or call-name index and reopen `src/api/log.js`. The rollback preserves the old lookup route; it does not promote the old judgment again. The references in the old revision and the old page records should both be retained, so the next attempt can distinguish whether the entry changed, the page produced no result, or the result was not copied down.

If the old index can still find the file but the page has no Logs with Changed Lines, first distinguish between two situations: the page action produced no result, or a result was produced but no record was left. Neither can be written as meaning that the entry does not exist. If the index does not match the reference to `v_prev`, stop treating the file as the sole entry and wait for new material from the same revision. If `path` has a value but `row` or `mode` was not recorded, the rollback should go only as far as preserving what was seen on the page; do not supply the meanings of the fields.

If another revision is used later for a new check, continue marking the old entry with its old time point, and state the revision change in the new entry. Do not put the result of the new verification into the old paragraph just to make the migration look continuous. The value of this page is preserving "where the search started at the time" and "where it stopped later," not stitching the two searches into a successful route without a break point.

## Boundary with another record

DOC-21 handles Merge Baseline Dominance. It can serve as navigation to related verification material, but does not replace the review of the log page here. This page retains only Logs with Changed Lines, `src/api/log.js`, the old revision reference, and the verification steps for moving from name search to the page action. Merge Baseline itself is not expanded on this page.

Both pages may be opened during the same compatibility review, but they serve different purposes: DOC-21 records object relationships in baseline verification, while this page records verification of the log display and migration entry. Do not copy the judgment from one page to the other merely because both pages contain `commit`.

The following sentence is still preserved according to the old page's wording:

> The old investigation record pointed here from the issue name and call name; the actual relationship still follows the reference for that revision.

It describes how the old entry was used, not a guarantee for the current path. Also retained alongside it is the operating habit from that time: first look at `log`, then use `path` and `row` to cross-check, and finally view `mode`. This sequence can continue to serve as the starting point for a lookup, but every location must have its own result record.

These are not blanks to be filled with speculation. If material is added later, append it only at the corresponding checkpoint; do not rewrite the old time point.

This page is therefore suitable to be treated as a legacy migration page that people may still open: it is possible to find the starting point from `src/api/log.js`, review the material using `v_prev`, know which fields the page review must preserve, and see where a compatibility conclusion has not yet been reached.

# Decision Record for stash Locking and Round Trips

The initial draft left a narrow decision: within the scope of Integrity Window 1.0, stash locking and the result after a single operation round trip would, for now, be kept in the same record. At the time, there was not enough material to identify what kind of mechanism the lock belonged to, nor was there any basis for treating the status terms that appeared after apply as a uniform result. In retrospect, the draft's wording is still useful, but it needs to be expanded from a working judgment into a decision that can continue to be used.

The early investigation mentioned stash, apply, and modified together in the same context. This grouping was not in itself an implementation sequence or an interface promise; it only showed that the issue at the time did not separate the three. If locking were first assigned to resource management and round trips to state management, later readers would receive two seemingly complete sets of material, yet be unable to tell whether they described the same operation. Retaining a shared entry point at least requires supplementary material to answer: which entry point was used, and what was observed under which version.

`src/api/stash.js` remains a point to revisit. The old record points to that path through the issue and call names, so it is useful for bringing the reading back to the local stash declarations and nearby code. It does not automatically identify the caller, nor can it state the version or result on the caller's behalf. The draft's warning, "do not treat a filename as a conclusion," went only this far: a path has navigational value, but the presence of a path is not a basis for expanding a local name into an explanation of behavior at every entry point.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

The first approach was to keep separate records. Locking would be listed on its own, round trips on their own, each awaiting supporting material. The advantage was that each record would be short and assignment would be straightforward; the problem was that the relationship that originally needed verification would be removed. One person might add only observations around the lock, while another might add only the result after apply. Neither record would be wrong, but neither would leave a place to put them into the same call context. For this requirement, separating them would not be more precise, but would establish the boundary prematurely.

The second approach was to write out a processing flow directly from `src/api/stash.js`. This was not adopted. A source code path can narrow the starting point for reading, but it cannot let the documentation bypass the actual call context. In particular, the term "round trip" does not in itself specify a concrete call sequence; "lock" does not specify where it is acquired or released either. If nearby elements in the file were rewritten as a complete flow, the later appearance of different entry points would force a revision to an explanation that should never have been fixed in place.

The third approach was to retain locking and round trips as a joint verification item, with supplementary material organized by context. The third approach was adopted. "Joint" here does not mean that the two necessarily happen at the same time, but that, until there are counterexamples, they should not be assumed up front to come from two unrelated requirement threads. If material mentions only modified, or only locking, without identifying where it enters the stash-related flow, it can still be retained as a lead, but it is not enough to change this decision.

This choice also avoids another misreading: interpreting a joint record as requiring every caller to perform the same reproduction. That is not necessary. What would really be valuable is having at least one caller that still uses the object and can provide the version, entry point, and current result together. It might support the draft's judgment that the records should be combined, or show that the early records mixed two entry points together; either outcome is more useful than filling in semantics based on names.

## Retained Judgment

The decision is not "locking and round trips must be related," but "do not treat them as unrelated until the call context has been established." This wording may seem conservative, but it has in fact affected how subsequent material is filed.

- If changes around the lock are not accompanied by results from before and after the same stash operation, record them as local observations for now.
- If results after apply are not accompanied by material on the lock, record them as observations on the round-trip side for now.
- When both appear together, the record must include the call entry point and version, not just a status term.
- If counterexamples show that the two come from different entry points, retain the original judgment to combine them in the historical section, then consider splitting the records, rather than silently rewriting the old paragraph to say something else.

The cost of handling things this way is that this page cannot provide a simplified interface description. Nor can it determine success criteria for any caller. This cost is acceptable, because the purpose of this page is not to label the observations immediately, but to prevent the same set of leads from losing their cross-reference paths after being split up.

The draft ended by asking whether the caller treats the status after apply as its own success criterion. This question remains unanswered. It should not be rewritten as "usually yes" or "usually no." What the status means to a caller depends on what that entry point actually passes to subsequent logic; without that context, any generalization would replace the subject of the investigation with speculation.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending
    state "stash Lock and Round Trip\nPending verification" as Pending
    state "Caller context" as Caller
    state "Version, entry point, current result" as Record
    Pending --> Caller: Add caller details
    Caller --> Record: Record context
    Record --> Pending: Relationship still needs to be determined
```

The states in the diagram are not a runtime flow. They only represent the order in which this page records supplementary material when it receives it: first return to the same item pending verification, then locate the caller context, and finally record the version, entry point, and result together. If the last item is missing, the material is not discarded, but neither is it used to redefine locking or round trips.

## Follow-up After Reassessment

IGT-218 turned the gap into a concrete investigation: find a caller still using "stash Lock and Round Trip" and verify its actual version, entry point, and current result. This matches the format for supplementary material required by the draft, so the card can serve as a navigational entry point for further investigation. The card is not a substitute for this page's technical conclusions; it gives the unfinished caller verification a place to continue.

According to the record, IGT-218 conducted a capacity reassessment on 2025-10-20. On 2025-10-21, the card moved from pending to review, on the grounds that implementation had already been completed on an existing branch and could go directly to review. These need to be viewed as two separate levels. The former shows that the investigation had been rescheduled, while the latter shows that an implementation entered review at that time; neither filled in the caller's actual version, entry point, and result. The reassessment therefore did not reinterpret "submitted for review" as meaning that stash behavior had been finalized.

The easiest mistake to make during review is to let work status stand in for technical judgment. Having the implementation on a branch does not mean that the caller has verified the lock's boundaries; moving the card into review does not mean that the status after apply now has a uniform meaning. Retaining the draft's open questions keeps these two facts distinct: work can continue moving forward without the documentation pretending that the gap has disappeared.

The reassessment also confirmed the boundary between this page and DOC-23. DOC-23 covers Package File Tail Check, Missing Pack Location Evidence, and delta and Object Format Boundary. These are all parallel discussions within the Integrity Window, but they do not explain stash locking or round trips. This page retains only this navigational relationship, to avoid piecing parallel topics together into a solution with no shared implementation basis.

## When Counterexamples Are Found Later

If the caller you find involves only one aspect of stash, for example if only the result can be seen and there is no material on locking, you must not fill in the other side just to make the record complete. Mark it as a one-sided context, and retain its relationship to the draft's judgment. Only when enough one-sided contexts have accumulated to show that their sources differ is there a reason to consider splitting the records.

Conversely, if a context includes both locking and the post-operation result, a relationship cannot be declared merely because the names match. At a minimum, it must be possible to identify the version and entry point; otherwise it has just one more term than the one-sided material, without any additional context on which to base a judgment. The bar here is not high, but it cannot be skipped, because this is exactly what distinguishes this decision from the early keyword-based investigation.

If counterexamples overturn the working premise of "keeping a joint record," the handling order has already been established: retain the old judgment, add the entry point indicated by the counterexample, explain why the records are being split, and then create separate follow-up records. Do not silently delete the early rationale for combining them. The early material did contain leads placing stash, apply, and modified in the same context; later discovering that they came from different entry points would only show that the original generalization was too broad, not that this history never happened.

Only one action remains at present: continue the investigation referenced by IGT-218 to find an identifiable caller. Once the version, entry point, and current result are available, this page can narrow the meaning of "round trip," confirm whether the lock appears in the same context, or withdraw the decision to keep a combined record. Until then, locking and round trips will continue to be retained as a single requirement thread pending verification.

This draft covers three adjacent issues in a single interface review: Package File Tail Check, Missing Pack Location Evidence, and delta and Object Format Boundary. The initial working hypothesis was to run the tail check first; if the packfile itself is incomplete, report the missing location at that same point. One puts all three checks on a single read path, so callers handle only one result; the cost is that tail corruption, a missing packfile, and an unrecognized object format may be conflated into the same type of error. The other retains three local checks, recording separately whether the packfile is readable, whether the candidate location matches, and whether the object is a processable delta or normal-format object; the cost is a longer interface, and existing callers need to adapt item by item. The second is tentatively preferred, but the names of the public fields and the error ordering have not been decided.

The minimum verification should use a real directory tree, rather than making assumptions from just a single packfile. Start from the repository root, retain the final match list, and then verify whether each candidate path remains reachable. Processing delta cannot in turn prove that the packfile location is correct; object-format boundaries cannot substitute for the tail check either.

Rollback conditions: If the added checks make old packages unreadable, or if callers can only accept a combined error, first revert the changes to the unified entry point and retain the local review record. The wording in the release notes and user documentation has not yet been checked.

# Packfile and Object Format Proposal

The old draft made a somewhat premature call: put Package File Tail Check first and assume it could also account for Missing Pack Location Evidence. At that point, the directory tree had not been rechecked, and there were not enough object samples to show that these three boundaries could share one set of return semantics. That assessment is retained here because it explains why the initial proposal did not handle delta separately; it cannot be treated as a finalized interface decision.

The entry point for rechecking is unchanged: `internal/iso-core`'s `src/storage/readObjectPacked.js`. This is a useful place to confirm declarations and adjacency relationships around the read path, not to assign implementation ownership based on file location alone. The proposal addresses three issues that often come up together in review but rely on different kinds of evidence: whether the end of the packfile is intact, where a missing pack is actually found, and whether object content falls within the format boundary for ordinary objects or deltas.

**Boundaries to retain initially**

Tail validation can only establish whether the end of a packfile meets expectations; it cannot establish whether the repository has another usable pack. For location evidence, collect candidate paths starting at the repository root and retain the final list of matches; "not found at the first location" does not mean "the pack does not exist." Format assessment must examine the object itself and its delta relationships; a path lookup with no match cannot stand in for it.

Two candidate interface shapes therefore remain. The combined approach folds all three result categories into a single read result, making integration quicker for users but making it hard for callers to distinguish corruption, absence, and format incompatibility. The split approach records a separate result for each of the three assessments. Callers need additional branches, but the location evidence needed for later diagnosis is retained. No record shows that either approach has been run successfully against a release package, so the split approach is presented here as a direction to try, not a decision.

**Rechecked cases**

The action recorded in IGT-219 was to place "Package File Tail Check" in a minimal but real directory tree and check whether each candidate path was still reachable. This adds a layer of path conditions beyond validating an isolated file directly, and exposes the risk in the old draft's treatment of tail and location issues together. The requirement in IGT-220 for this part is to follow "Missing Pack Location Evidence" from the repository root, retain the final list of matches, and not replace results with internal guesses. Both records support observing the results separately first, but do not yet specify public interface fields.

IGT-221 calls for checking how "delta and Object Format Boundary" is currently described in release notes, user documentation, and templates, and listing the specific files that need changes. This extends the issue from the read implementation to user-facing wording: even if the individual checks work, users will still handle failures based on their old understanding if the documentation continues to describe deltas and ordinary objects as the same category. For this part of the migration, there are only files awaiting review, with no change list to cite.

**Trial sequence**

First select a minimal directory tree that includes packfiles and object relationships, and record the tail-check result, the list of candidate locations, and the format assessment result separately. Do not collapse the three results into a single error in the first round. Then use the same tree to check whether callers actually need to combine branches; if they do, retain the original classification at the caller boundary rather than keeping only a generic failure.

For delta-related rechecks, record the input object and the location of the pack it depends on separately. Successfully parsing a delta does not mean the packfile has passed tail validation; passing tail validation does not mean the object format necessarily falls within the scope supported in this round. No format enums or error field names are frozen here, so fields are not filled in ahead of time and candidate results are not presented as compatibility commitments.

**Items retained after review**

The old approach still has one practical advantage: doing tail validation early makes it easy to stop further parsing on failure and keeps the diagnostic sequence short. Its disadvantage is equally clear: once "pack does not exist," "pack exists but its tail is abnormal," and "object format mismatch" share a single error path, the location evidence required by IGT-220 is lost, leaving later investigation to guess the paths again. The split approach comes at the cost of additions to both the interface and the migration documentation, and existing callers Fang Ke may only be prepared to handle one type of failure.

This page therefore does not declare the work complete. The only decisions that can be recorded at this point are: delta results must not replace location evidence during rechecks; the final list of matches for candidate paths must be retained; and the three assessments must be recorded separately during the trial phase. Whether to combine them into a public return value, the order of the combined fields, and how existing callers need to migrate still await review of the specific call relationships and documentation.

**Rollback conditions and open items**

If the added checks prevent continued use of old packs in existing read scenarios, or if existing callers can only consume a combined error, revert the unified-entry-point changes and retain the local rechecks and the original read path for now. If the minimal directory tree does not yield repeatable candidate paths, stay at the location-evidence stage rather than inferring the reason for the missing pack from the tail-validation result. If the format samples are insufficient to distinguish ordinary objects from deltas, do not put unconfirmed boundaries into the release notes either.

# Tag Filtering and Remote Credential Migration Notes

We originally grouped tag advertisements and remote credentials because, during investigation, both led back to the area around `src/api/tag.js`. After review, this wording caused a misreading: because the filtering result showed no anomaly, it was taken to mean that calls to remote URL were covered as well. IGT-224 corresponds to Ad Filtering After tag Stripping. The check must not infer backward from filtered output; it should start with the pre-call state. # tag Filtering and Remote Credential Migration Notes

This page retains two compatibility migration tracks: Ad Filtering After tag Stripping, and Remote URL and Credentials at the public entry point. They once shared a comparison only because the old investigation could trace the same set of tag/ref call names back to the area around `src/api/tag.js`. This shared starting point was later misread as shared pass criteria, making the old steps appear to cover more than they actually did.

They remain on the same page so that the reason these two tracks were once grouped together is still visible during migration; however, the materials, stop points, and restoration points for each review should be kept separate. `src/api/tag.js` serves only as a starting point for investigation around the tag/ref names. It helps trace old investigation records back to the relevant calls, but does not mean that credential handling belongs to the tag file, nor does it require remote checks to start with implementation details.

The earliest records required only that the pre-call state be captured first. This practice remains: without the ref values, advertisement state, and entry-point information visible before the call, it is difficult to determine whether the filtered result reflects an expected reduction or additional changes. Reconstructing the prior state after changes have occurred usually only mixes observations from two different points in time.

## Retained Legacy Steps

The following passage is an operational note originally retained with the migration. It has not been deleted because some callers still prepare their comparisons in this order; its combined assessment is no longer applicable.

> First follow Ad Filtering After tag Stripping; if the output shows no anomalies, use the results of the same call to confirm Remote URL and Credentials. If neither side has any new visible items, the migration can be considered complete.

The problem with this note is not the observation of "whether there are any new visible items." Advertisement filtering does need to retain this observation. The problem is that it puts visible advertisement changes and remote entry-point coverage into a single results sheet: stable advertisements after filtering only indicate that this particular advertisement comparison did not immediately reveal a difference; an example triggering the remote URL only indicates that the example reached the entry point. Neither observation is sufficient to draw a conclusion about the other side.

The old steps have been retired. When restoring the old invocation, its practice of saving the pre-call state can still be used; a single output must no longer be used to sign off on both migration tracks. The phrase "the same call" in the old records makes it especially easy to overlook this distinction: occurring in the same call does not mean the same behavior has been checked.

## Prepare Two Separate Records First

Before starting the migration, divide the items to investigate into an advertisement-filtering record and a remote-entry record. They can use call materials prepared in the same session, but should not be written into the same notes field.

The advertisement-filtering record should retain the ref values and advertisement state visible before the call; indicate whether this call entered the tag-stripping path; then record which items remain visible after completion, and whether there are any additional visible changes that were not present before the call. If a difference is found, add one more detail: whether it appeared when filtering completed or only after subsequent adjacent calls. This point determines whether the next step is to restore the filtering branch or continue investigating adjacent calls.

The remote-entry record should contain only the remote URL entry point currently in use, whether existing tests or examples actually passed through the entry point, whether credentials entered the path under investigation through this invocation of the entry point, and the user paths that the examples have not yet reached. There is no need to extract "apparently normal" snippets from advertisement output here, nor to guess where credentials went just to fill out the record.

Keeping two separate records does not require preparing two environments. It simply rejects writing "ran in the same invocation" as "the same behavior has been proven." If the pre-call state cannot be saved, do not switch to the tag-stripping path yet; if an example only triggers URL without confirming the path taken by the credentials, do not record the remote credential migration as complete either.

## Migration Sequence for Advertisement Filtering

First establish a comparison using the pre-call state. The comparison needs to show the ref values and advertisement state at that time, then run Ad Filtering After tag Stripping, and examine only the changes left by this path. The question here is not whether the output is shorter than before, nor whether only one type of name remains; it is whether filtering introduced visible items that did not exist before the call, or also removed items that should have been retained.

Additional visible items can easily be attributed to the remote entry point because the two tracks once shared the same results. If this happens, stop at the advertisement-filtering record first. Compare the pre-call state, the state after filtering completed, and the state after subsequent adjacent calls again. If the difference already existed when filtering completed, a remote example will not explain it; if the difference appeared only later, the filtering result should not be directly recorded as anomalous either.

When the before-and-after changes can be explained, retain the correspondence between the prior state and the result, and mark this particular run of the tag-stripping path as reviewed. "Reviewed" here applies only to this specific comparison, not to ref combinations that did not occur. When both tag and other ref values are present before the call, which changes after filtering are expected must still be determined from the actual pre-call state.

When a difference cannot be explained, revert to the old invocation method. Reverting does not mean deleting the comparisons already collected; it means stopping use of the new path for this migration. Retain the input for that run, the pre-call state, and the visible items after completion, and repeat the comparison from the same point next time. Do not change the remote URL first, or substitute another existing example to cover this advertisement difference; doing so would only move the problem from the filtering record to the other track.

IGT-224 is the starting point for taking inventory of Ad Filtering After tag Stripping. Some parts remain unconfirmed as the work progresses, so the stop point of "revert to the old invocation if a difference cannot be explained" remains here. This stop point addresses only advertisement filtering itself and should not be rewritten as a remote credential anomaly.

## Migration Sequence for the Remote Entry Point

Once advertisement filtering has its own comparison, address Remote URL and Credentials. First take a test or example already used by the current public entry point and have the remote URL pass through that entry point. Then confirm whether this example brought credentials to the path that needs to be checked. The purpose of this sequence is not to enforce an order, but to make both URL and the credentials traceable to the same entry-point record.

An existing example passing through the remote URL does not mean that credentials necessarily took the same path. Earlier records described "URL was triggered" as "Remote URL and Credentials is covered"; the wording should now match the strength of the observation: when only URL has been confirmed, record that URL was triggered; only when the destinations of both URL and the credentials are clear should the entry point be marked as reviewed. Leaving the credentials section blank is not missing documentation, but marks the point from which the next check should continue using the existing example.

Conversely, the advertisement-filtering comparison cannot fill gaps for the remote entry point either. No additional visible changes in the filtered advertisements only means that this particular filtering result can be explained; it does not indicate whether the example carried credentials, much less whether user paths not reached by the example have passed through the entry point.

IGT-225 is used to collect these gaps. The card covers user paths not yet covered by existing tests or examples when the current public entry point supports Remote URL and Credentials. Writing the uncovered items back to IGT-225 allows the next review to continue from the actual entry point, rather than working backward from the previous advertisement results. It is not a rollback record for the filtering branch.

When the remote branch needs to be restored, retain the existing example in use and the entry-point observations already confirmed, rather than undoing them together with the prior state for advertisement filtering. The goal of restoration is to return to a pre-migration entry-point state from which investigation can continue, not to claim that a conclusion has been reached about the credential path.

```text
Old combined record

Pre-call state
    |
    +-- Ad Filtering After tag Stripping --+
    |                          +--> One combined assessment
    +-- Remote URL and Credentials -------+

Separated records

Pre-call state --> Ad Filtering After tag Stripping --> Advertisement-change comparison
                                      |
                                      +--> Difference cannot be explained: revert to the old invocation method

Existing remote entry point --> URL and credential checks -----> Entry-path comparison
                                      |
                                      +--> URL triggered, credentials unconfirmed: record the gap
```

The two main tracks in the diagram do not impose a strict execution order. In practice, the remote example can be obtained first, or the pre-call advertisement state can be obtained first. What must be maintained is that results go back to their respective records: advertisement differences go back to the filtering comparison, and entry-point gaps go back to the remote record, rather than being combined into a single "compatibility passed" result at the end.

## Locations to Revisit and Adjacent Records

When encountering the tag/ref names or old investigation records, first review the related calls around `src/api/tag.js`, then return to the saved pre-call state. This location only helps locate adjacent points around advertisement filtering. Checks for Remote URL and Credentials should still start from the current public entry point and existing tests or examples; do not record the two as belonging to the same implementation just because they appear in the same compatibility check.

For the verification design of Recursive Directory Creation Retries, see DOC-26. It can be consulted as an adjacent migration record, but directory-creation retries do not provide a basis for assessing advertisement filtering or remote credentials here. If directory-related behavior appears during review, first separate it from the two comparisons, then continue handling it in DOC-26, to prevent new adjacent behavior from being folded into a combined result again.

The two cards also have different outputs. IGT-224 retains the comparison of states before and after advertisement filtering, along with differences that remain unexplained; IGT-225 retains which remote entry points have been triggered by existing examples and which user paths remain untouched. Their appearing together does not mean they have the same acceptance target.

One item remains unresolved: when both tag and other ref values appear in the pre-call state, which changes after filtering should be considered expected must continue to be reviewed for each specific call. The old draft tried to borrow answers from remote examples, but this was later found to conflate entry-point coverage with advertisement changes. The current requirement is only to retain the question together with the pre-call state; without a specific comparison, do not present it as a general conclusion.

# Docs site dual-state incident postmortem

This incident involved the same object in tests · User Documentation Portal. The entry point reported different current revisions at two sampling points; the working-tree contents also differed from the old records. No signs that the object had been replaced were found at the time, but the differences were enough to leave the version notes and handling of outdated content without a common basis.

The docs site isn't an ancillary page of the main project. It provides a user entry point for tests, maintains its own version notes and handling of outdated content, and has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. For that reason, this incident wasn't folded into routine working-tree diff handling. The entry-point records, old records, and post-recovery page were kept separately.

## Sequence of observations

The first thing observed was a mismatch between the working tree and the old records. The initial hunch was that the working tree hadn't been cleaned up, and checks started in that direction. That assessment only explained the differences seen locally; it couldn't explain why the entry point listed the same object as the current revision at both points in time.

After that, the entry point wasn't repeatedly refreshed. Further retries would mix new page states into the original observations, making it impossible to tell whether the difference came from updates on the page side, lag in the records, or changes on both sides. Records of the version seen at the time were preserved, and the last-seen value was no longer used to overwrite the previous one.

Once the post-recovery page was available, object consistency could be restored: the entry point, the original record, and the post-recovery target no longer required readers to treat the two states as two objects. "Recovery" here only means that the docs site could once again organize its notes around a single object, not that the reason for the commit-pointer change had been found.

When the records were organized, the initial "working tree not cleaned up" explanation was downgraded to an investigative starting point. It hadn't been confirmed as the cause and wasn't enough to explain the sequence of the two current-revision records. The original record still retains this starting point so later readers won't assume it was clear from the outset where the problem lay.

## Scope of impact

The affected areas were the version reference shown by the docs site entry point, and the version notes and outdated-content decisions based on that reference. Viewed at just one of the two points in time, the page could appear normal; viewed side by side, the two observations gave readers different current versions. This difference left users unable to confirm which set of notes to follow and left no stable reference for deciding whether old content should be retired.

The behavior of adjacent projects wasn't included in the impact scope at the time. The tests entry point itself, the version notes it stored, and the handling of outdated content around that entry point are the parts this record can confirm. The value ultimately shown on the page after recovery also wasn't treated as a complete history: it could only show the state observed later, not fill in the missing interval.

The docs site's maintenance plan therefore retained two actions. One was to freeze the entry-point record from the incident; the other was to save the post-recovery page separately. Neither could substitute for the other: the former preserved what things looked like when the difference occurred, while the latter preserved what they looked like after object consistency had been restored. Combining the two into a single "recovered" conclusion would erase the sequence this incident most needed to preserve.

## Unresolved points

The records don't explain why the commit pointer changed. There were no usable intermediate observations to connect the first difference and the recovered state into a continuous sequence; the missing points in time remain blank. There is also no evidence showing whether the change occurred during entry-point generation, in the docs site's records, or at an earlier object-update stage.

The call at the time was to stop further retries, not to declare the root cause found. This stopping point reduced contamination of the original observations from further page changes and made it possible to retain both "object consistency restored" and "cause unknown" after recovery. It was a choice made for this one docs site incident and should not be extended into a general rule for other entry points.

The original is stored at `docs/adj-tests/incidents/tests-user-documentation-portal-same-object-two-states.md`. The old records, post-recovery page, and unconfirmed cause are retained there, each tied to its own point in time. If intermediate records become available later, first fill in the timeline between the two current revisions, then assess whether the initial working-tree hypothesis still has any value; do not directly replace the records retained during the incident with content from the post-recovery page.

## Earlier wording retained

At the time, "the object is now consistent" was written after the recovery action. That statement only meant that the docs site could once again organize its notes around the same object. It did not mean that the version history was consistent, much less that a commit-pointer change had been ruled out. The earlier wording wasn't deleted because it explains why those on duty stopped retrying; when looking back now, read it alongside the unknowns above.

This postmortem is retained as an incident record for the docs site. Whether there is a relationship between the missing interval, the reason for the pointer change, and the working-tree differences remains unconfirmed in this record.

# Resource Site Routing Change Proposal

When this proposal was first documented, the resource site treated replay records and index snapshots as two outputs from the same entry point. On a later review, the problem wasn't the naming but that, when users encountered blank content, they had too little information to tell whether the process had not been recorded or whether no searchable index had been formed at a particular point in time. Those two cases should lead to different follow-up checks.

The original proposal is therefore retained as a limited pilot: replay records are not replaced; a candidate entry point for index snapshots is added alongside them. The candidate entry point is not responsible for explaining the entire history; it should only preserve the material that was visible at a given moment. Replay records remain for reviewing the process. If the missing-data path for each can be identified, the resource site's maintenance records do not need to treat "no content" as a single type of failure.

A green page is not the pass condition for the pilot. What matters is not whether the display is complete, but whether a user following the current entry point can distinguish the following situations: no record; a record that points to an old object; the periods before and after the entry-point change fall into different measurement windows; or collection and execution were never enabled in the first place. Without additional explanation, the last two are easily misread as the index itself having failed.

The follow-up action specified in IGTA-002 is specific: first find the person on duty and verify the gap in the current revision; if there is no record, state that it cannot be determined. This requirement shaped the boundary of the candidate entry point. The index snapshot must not fabricate content that does not exist just to make the result look continuous, nor may it present speculation beyond the on-duty records as a definite result.

IGTA-006 makes the original two-week comparison no longer straightforward. Statistics from before and after the current entry-point change cannot be subtracted directly; once the entry point changed, the material visible before and after it was not naturally a continuous sample set. The earlier idea was to use a trend to determine whether the candidate entry point was easier to locate; that can now only be retained as an idea pending validation. The toolchain is already fixed, but that does not solve the changed comparison baseline.

The handoff was not completed as originally planned. The due action associated with IGTA-004 still matches, but the current result retained in the card was an old result; after the backfill work started, the item was returned to the queue. The pilot therefore cannot assume that the person handing it off, the person taking it over, and the confirmation time will all be provided in the same window. If those records are incomplete, even a candidate entry point that appears can only be treated as a local sample; it cannot support declaring the original entry point ready for retirement.

Another blocker is that the old-version images have already been cleaned up. The original proposal intended to review the old material alongside the new entry to verify whether the split had lost historical readability; if the required images are unavailable, this part cannot be reconstructed from memory. Keeping this blocker is more useful than continuing to assume that every old version can be retrieved at any time.

The review asked for a contrasting input. Here, that does not mean just finding a failed item; it means a piece of the same type of material where the replay record can explain it but the index snapshot cannot, or the reverse. Only when that difference appears can we tell that the split truly exposed responsibilities that had previously been mixed together, rather than adding another entry point with a different name.

Rollback remains a minimal action: stop further piloting of the candidate entry point and retain the replay record as the original entry point; index snapshots already retained are not automatically rewritten as replay results. Whether these snapshots should be deleted must wait until the gaps involving the lock-order caller and the old-version comparison have been answered. The resource site's trigger records still need to trace the actual action to identify the person taking over; groups that have been taken offline will no longer be used as new entry points.
