# Proposal to Adjust the Resource Site Approach

The resource site once handled "being able to review a process" and "being able to find material from a particular point in time" through the same entry point. There appeared to be only one entry point, but in practice it left two different kinds of gaps: sometimes the process itself was not recorded, and sometimes the process existed but there was no index available for lookup at that point in time. Early organization efforts mixed these two kinds of gaps together, and subsequent follow-up checks often left only old objects or old results.

This proposal did not become a replacement plan. It preserves a separation approach that was considered at the time but later not adopted, along with the reasons it was not made standard practice. Replay records and index snapshots both remain under discussion; the resource site's need for a clearer entry point must not be used to assume, in retrospect, that separating them has already resolved recording, statistics, or handoff issues.

## What Was Initially Intended to Be Separated

`Replay records` are suited to answering "what happened at the time". They depend on the processes, actions, and sequences already recorded. Users reviewing history through this approach may see a history with gaps, or one that still points to old objects; this does not automatically mean that the material does not exist.

`Index snapshots` were conceived differently. They should no longer be responsible for replaying processes, but should retain only the content that the resource site could retrieve at a particular point in time. If there is no snapshot for a given point in time, the entry point should allow that absence to remain, rather than filling it with content from a later time. The value of this is not a tidier page, but different follow-up handling for "no index was created" and "the process was not recorded".

The initial assessment was: separate index snapshots from replay records, and separate their failure-handling paths accordingly. For replay records, gaps should be traced back to the process and on-duty records; for index snapshots, the first step should be to confirm whether retrievable content should exist for that point in time. The two paths should no longer be lumped together under the same phrase, "material not found".

This assessment was only a candidate arrangement. The current lock-ordering callers had not yet been identified, so it was not known whether separating the entry point would change the order of existing calls. Rollback was also unresolved: the early version had no answer as to whether restoring the old entry point would be enough, or whether index snapshots already generated would also need to be handled.

## The Original Trial Concept

The candidate entry point was not originally intended to be a second, complete resource site. It was only meant to appear alongside the original entry point, retaining replay records without moving the existing process descriptions. The purpose was to let the same type of material reveal its own gaps in each entry point, not to pursue a one-step replacement.

The comparison needed for the trial was also narrow: when looking for the same material through the two entry points, could users distinguish among three outcomes, "no record", "a record exists but points to an old object", and "no snapshot exists for that point in time". If all they still got was a blank, the separation would merely have renamed the entry points without reducing misjudgments.

The two-week window was proposed at the time to avoid looking at just one successful query. That window ultimately did not yield a valid conclusion, because the current entry point had changed. Statistics from before and after the entry-point change cannot be directly subtracted: the material sources and lookup paths on the two sides were no longer under the same set of conditions. Connecting the before-and-after numbers into a single trend would mistake the entry-point change for an effect of the candidate approach.

The toolchain was frozen at one point, originally in the hope of stopping further drift in the comparison. But freezing the toolchain only shows that one condition did not keep changing during the comparison; it is no substitute for knowing when the entry point changed, nor does it show whether the old material can still be obtained. This part was therefore not treated as a result supporting the separation.

## Context That Could Not Be Fully Reconstructed

The follow-up check requirements in IGTA-002 narrowed the scope: first contact the person on duty to verify the gaps in the current revision; if there is no record, explicitly state that no determination can be made. This requirement rejected a seemingly convenient practice—inferring what must have happened at the time from content indexed later. Candidate index snapshots can retain content that has been seen, but cannot turn unknown points in time into known ones.

Historical comments on the same card also noted that the action scheduled for the due time still pointed to yesterday's object. This shows that actions at the entry point and the material objects may change at different rates. Even if the candidate entry point displays new content, that does not establish that the object being tracked has switched over. For the resource site, an old object is not a formatting issue; it leads follow-up checks back to the wrong context.

IGTA-004 exposed a handoff gap. Backfilling had started, but was later returned to the queue; at the time, only the action scheduled for the due time could be matched up, while the card's so-called current result was still an old result. The original proposal assumed that the person handing it off, the person taking it over, and the confirmation time would be available by the end of the trial, but that assumption did not hold. Without a handoff record, observations from a period of using the candidate entry point cannot be attributed to a stable maintenance activity.

The trial should therefore not use "someone saw the result" as its completion criterion. If a result has no corresponding confirmation time and no actual person taking it over, it only shows that content was displayed somewhere on the resource site at some point, not that the entry point remained usable after the handoff. The approach proposed in IGTA-013 was to follow the post-trigger actions to find the person who actually took over, and remove already-offline groups from the new entry point; this should be completed before discussing who should maintain the candidate entry point.

The blocker recorded in IGTA-006 was more direct: the required old-version image had already been cleaned up. The early concept called for checking old material side by side with candidate index snapshots to confirm that the separation had not obscured history. When the image is unavailable, screenshots, recollections, or old links cannot substitute for this check. Continuing to claim that a complete comparison is possible would only disguise unavailable old content as existing evidence.

This also explains why "index snapshots are easier to find" was not stated as a conclusion. For some points in time, it is still impossible to determine whether material should exist; for others, the old version cannot be reviewed again. Neither type of unknown supports ranking one approach above the other, only retaining the original entry point and stopping any expansion of the trial.

## Reasons Rejected During Review

"The page looks more modern" is not a reason for adoption. If the resource site's entry point becomes clearer but the gaps remain hidden together, users will instead have a harder time knowing whether to follow up on on-duty records, index generation, or handoff records. A visual cleanup does not mean that the relationships among the materials have been separated.

"A single successful query" is not a reason for adoption either. Finding material once may simply mean that the object happened to have a recorded process, or happened to have a snapshot. It does not test the opposite cases: replay records can explain something that index snapshots cannot, or an index snapshot is visible while the process is missing. The review required retaining these contrasting inputs precisely to avoid treating an incidental success as an advantage of the approach.

"The old entry point has problems, so just remove it" was likewise not accepted. The old entry point carries replay records; the candidate entry point handles index snapshots at most. Removing it outright would also cut off processes that could previously be reviewed, and expand the scope of impact before the lock-ordering callers had been verified.

Another proposal was to fill points in time that had no collection results with zeros, making the index appear continuous. The checks in IGTA-011 required first verifying whether collection and execution were enabled; no zeros should be filled in when the current entry point has no evidence. A zero value is not the same as no record, and the former would add unconfirmed meaning to trends and users' judgments.

## Rolling Back Does Not Mean Deleting History

The rollback action in this proposal should always be smaller in scope than replacement: stop further trials of the candidate entry point, and retain replay records as the original entry point. This does not claim that the original entry point has no problems, but avoids losing the only process that can still be reviewed while the old-version image is missing and the handoff remains incomplete.

Index snapshots that already exist should not be rewritten as replay records, nor should they be deleted immediately just to leave the resource site with a single approach. They may be retained as partial material left by the candidate approach, but not as proof that "the trial passed". Whether to clean them up must wait for clear answers to two questions: what the current lock-ordering callers are; and whether retaining snapshots during rollback would mislead subsequent queries.

If the resource site considers separation again, it should first mark when the current entry point changed, to avoid directly subtracting before-and-after statistics; then separately confirm whether collection and execution are enabled. Without these prerequisites, any blank can only be recorded as unknown, rather than attributed to either index snapshots or replay records.

## The Assessment Retained at This Stage

The fact that this approach was not adopted does not mean there is no distinction between replay records and index snapshots. Their responsibilities remain different, especially when handling missing material, old objects, and expired results. The approach was not adopted because the conditions needed for the trial comparison were not all in place: the entry-point change interrupted the before-and-after trend, handoff records remained incomplete, and the old-version image had been cleaned up.

DOC-29 remains nearby reference material for locating the current entry point and current revision, but it does not replace the objections and rollback points retained on this page. IGTA-002, IGTA-004, and IGTA-006 record the follow-up checks, handoff, and image-related blocker; IGTA-011 and IGTA-013 retain the follow-up questions about collection status and the person who actually took over.

Two items remain undecided: the lock-ordering callers, and whether to retain index snapshots after rollback. Until these are confirmed, the two-week trial will not be restarted, nor will the candidate entry point be described as the resource site's established approach.

# Caller Integration Testing Window Checklist

This old checklist originally treated closing out the window as a very short wrap-up: retain the last output from the current entry point, return borrowed material, then confirm the rollback entry point. It was once used to handle a caller integration-testing window, so it remains here; but it does not cover subsequent windows, and a partial recovery must not be treated as the end of the entire integration session.

The old version's item 1 framed "seeing a compatibility window" as a signal that closeout could continue; item 3 also implied that caller evidence alone was enough to stop the live session. This wording is retained to explain why the checks were not split out at the time. Its defect is specific: a compatibility window was only one condition observed at the time; it cannot replace separate confirmation of the current entry point, last output, return action, and rollback status.

## Artifacts to leave before closeout

Open `docs/adj-utils/release/utils-caller-integration-short-checklist-before-window-end.md` first. This is still the artifact entry point left by this window; do not replace the records there with a release page with a similar name.

1. **Pin the current entry point.** Record the entry point in use and the current revision to be examined in this run. If the entry point changes, the earlier output may remain as a historical sample, but it cannot be treated as part of the same comparison as output from the new entry point.
2. **Retain the last output.** Keep the first result that was visible alongside the last output before closeout. If the live setup was changed midway for diagnosis, record it in a separate entry; a cleaned-up result must not overwrite the original last output.
3. **Log borrowed items and returns.** List each item borrowed for this run, who will accept its return, and the latest return deadline. If no explicit return deadline is available, do not check off closeout; writing only "handle later" does not count.
4. **Keep the rollback entry point.** While the last output is still viewable, confirm that the rollback entry point for adj-utils has not been removed prematurely. This confirms only that the entry point is still there, not that rollback is complete.

The four items above were originally written on one line; do not substitute one for another in practice. For example, the existence of the last output does not prove that the borrowed material has been returned; an available rollback entry point does not prove that the caller has exited the current entry point.

## How to compare within a window

If a rerun is needed, keep `utils-client-integration`, the current entry point, and the command fixed, and change only the current revision. Only then can the two resulting outputs be compared side by side. Keep records where the environment has changed, but do not call them a same-run comparison.

The old version once advised, "Do not clear the live setup after caller evidence is available." That statement is not wrong in itself; the problem is that it did not define what counted as caller evidence. Use the narrower interpretation here: if the execution record can be traced to the first broken link, stop at the current result; do not follow the broken link to infer the status of other packages. If the execution record does not reach a broken link, record the result as not yet reached instead of adding a success determination.

The package-tail check still belongs before closeout, rather than being filled in after rollback. It checks only whether the artifacts or status left by this run match the current entry point; a "success" in the logs is not enough to substitute for this check. If the package-tail check is unavailable, retain the last output and stop closeout; do not remove the entry point first and then go back to look for evidence.

## Where to actually stop

On any of the following, stop checking boxes, leave the live setup intact, and use the rollback entry point:

- The current entry point has changed, but the last output from the original entry point has not been retained;
- Borrowed material has no latest return deadline, or it is unclear who will accept its return;
- Only a partial recovery is visible, and the rollback entry point and exit action cannot be checked separately;
- During a rerun, the entry point or command was changed in addition to the current revision.

Stopping does not mean marking the window complete. First record which item number you stopped at, what remains in the live setup, and whether the rollback entry point is available. If the status of the rollback entry point and the exit action do not match, verify them separately; the fact that the exit action has occurred does not mean the rollback entry point has been restored, and vice versa. The old version grouped these two statuses under "partial recovery"; this is its most misleading point.

During rollback, do not clear the last output either. First use the recorded rollback entry point, then verify whether the exit action is still in the state recorded for this run. If rollback changes the live setup, keep a separate copy of the post-rollback output; do not use it to replace the last output from before rollback. If there is no original output available for comparison, record rollback only as executed; do not use that to write a recovery conclusion.

## Items for subsequent windows

The IGTC-008 card records that the current integration-testing content and exit action must be exported before switching environments; after the environment changes, do not call it a same-run comparison. The IGTC-009 card specifies a rerun with the entry point and command fixed, changing only the current revision. The IGTC-010 card checks the rollback entry point and the exit action separately. These three cards are itemized records added later; they do not turn the old checklist into a rule for all release windows.

The still-missing piece is the rollback test in the shared environment. The old version had no result for this item, yet wrote about the appearance of a compatibility window as if it were a completion signal; this assessment is retained so whoever takes over does not carry it forward.

# Caller Cache Decision Record

Integration testing had stopped at a still-readable `current revision`. What we could keep on hand was that run's output and the tail of the logs; rebuilding the environment at that point would have produced results from a new integration run, not a comparison against the original caller state. The cache was not a complete snapshot of that state, just a way to preserve this observation temporarily.

## Options considered at the time

1. Keep `current revision` and continue the comparison using it along with the existing output.
2. Rebuild the environment first, then look for differences in the new call results.
3. Remove the old entry point outright and clear the cache along with it.

The second option looked clean, but it would have changed the conditions being compared. The question at the time was what the caller had left under the original conditions, not whether utils-client-integration could be integrated again, so we did not choose it. The third option had been deferred even earlier: once the old entry point was removed, the final output would also lose its point of reference.

We decided to keep the cache and `current revision`, without rebuilding the environment for this comparison. This did not mean treating the cache as a long-term runtime environment; at the time, we accepted it only as a working reference for a single, limited comparison. Any later validation of a new caller should have its own record, rather than adding new results as though they had already been observed in this round.

Reservations remained. Someone pointed out that it was still unclear exactly which callers were in use in the working tree. The cache could show only which results had been retained, not that all callers had gone through the same entry point. This objection was valid, but not enough to change the decision at the time: rebuilding would immediately lose the original conditions, while keeping the cache would at least let us inspect the differences in the same place.

At the time, no decision had been made on whether rollback should only restore the old entry point. If the exit action changes where the output or logs are retained, the original comparison should be considered over; do not use material from after caching to stand in for the original state. This constraint made the decision seem conservative, but it was more workable than cleaning up first and then guessing at the caller state.

For notes on a comparison from the same round that changed only the revision, see DOC-38. Decision materials are stored in `docs/adj-utils/decisions/utils-client-integration-cache-vs-original-state-tradeoff.md`; that location retains the naming and attachment links used at the time. After the later maintainer handoff, the outcome of the exit action still had not been added to this version.

# Postmortem: Two-State Package Integration Incident

The same object in api package integration work reported different current revisions at two points in time. The evidence retained by the caller also did not match the earlier record. This note starts by recording the incident against that object, without treating the two states as two separate objects or the earlier record as already invalid.

The entry point's version at the time and the original input were captured first. There were no further retries, because a retry could only produce new output, not recover the discrepancy seen the first time. The compatibility window could later be restored, but the restoration time could not stand in for the cause: why the replay record had changed was still unanswered at the time.

The available material is in three places: the original record, the recovery page, and a follow-up note with the cause still unconfirmed. All three concern the cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer integrations built around api; these objects have their own schedules, maintainers, and exit criteria. Adjacent services were not included in the causal chain; there was not enough evidence on hand to support that conclusion.

The impact that could be confirmed at the time was narrow: the state seen by the caller did not match the earlier record, so that record alone could not be used to determine whether the integration combination was still usable. Once the compatibility window was restored, the user flow could continue; that did not establish when the two versions started to diverge or whether the entry point changes came from the same modification.

The review starts at `docs/adj-api/incidents/api-package-integration-collaboration-same-object-two-states.md`. What's needed is not an after-the-fact explanation, but the time each of the two states appeared and which inputs were still retained before and after the replay record changed.

To add: the time between the two observation points.

# Package Integration Dual-State Failure Postmortem

This incident did not present as simply a failure or simply a recovery. The cross-package dependency around api left behind two states in the same integration round that both appeared to be "current": the entry point pointed to different current revisions at the two observation points; the daily report had also once combined two execution records into a single row; after the local result recovered, the public entry corresponding to the exit entry still failed. They occurred around the same object, but cannot be collapsed into a single root cause without evidence.

The object itself is not merely a call record. api-package-integration involves version combinations and consumer integration, and has its own schedule, owner, and exit criteria. When the anomaly appeared, the easiest mistake was to interpret a green result in one place as meaning the entire integration combination was already consistent, or to interpret an old record as the sole description of the current entry point. Neither interpretation was sufficient to explain what was observed.

The earliest retained version recorded a small but critical fork: the caller-side evidence differed from the old record; the entry point gave different current revisions at two points in time. The recorder preserved the original input and entry-point version, then stopped retrying. This stop was not because the cause had already been located, but because continuing to generate new results would overwrite the difference observed the first time. The compatibility window later recovered, but why the replay record changed remains unknown.

## The observed states were not all the same kind of thing

The materials for this incident contain at least four kinds of states. Their names are similar, but their meanings are different.

The first is entry-point state. It only indicates the current revision seen at a particular observation point; it does not indicate why another observation point differed, nor which version combination the consumer ultimately received. The two entry-point results were therefore preserved as-is, rather than selecting one to revise the old record.

The second is execution-record state. The daily report once merged two execution records, while the original ticket had no corresponding merged item. The merged single row makes it easy to think that the object underwent only one execution, or that one of the records was zero; a subsequent addendum explicitly noted that this was not zero, but that the collection record corresponding to the execution record had never arrived at all. What is missing here is the collection record, not a value that can be automatically derived from the summary row.

The third is path state. The local result recovered, while the public entry corresponding to the exit entry still failed; the two cannot substitute for each other. Local recovery means that this local path no longer produced the result seen at the time; the continued failure of the public entry means that at least one path serving the integrating party had not caught up. Their simultaneous existence is precisely why "the same object has two states" still needs to be retained in the latter half.

The fourth is recovery state. The fact that the compatibility window recovered was an actual observation, not confirmation of the root cause. It reduced the immediate impact of the integration interruption, but did not explain the difference in current revisions, why the daily report was merged, why the collection record never arrived, or why the public entry continued to show failure. The recovery page was therefore saved separately and was not used to fill in the earlier unknowns.

These states are related at the object level, but there is not enough material to establish a strict causal chain. In particular, the fact that the daily report was merged does not mean that it caused the entry-point difference; nor does the fact that the public entry still failed mean that the local recovery was ineffective. The postmortem preserves this asymmetry so that subsequent verification can continue to distinguish observations from judgments.

## Materials left behind in sequence

The initial record preserved only the conflict among the current object, the earlier record, and the caller's evidence. It did not include complete timestamps, nor did it present guesses about neighboring services as causes. This choice later proved useful: if every peripheral observation had been woven into an explanation from the outset, it would have been difficult, when later splitting the merged rows in the daily report, to tell which content came from the input and which was merely conjecture at the time.

The original record is saved in `docs/adj-api/incidents/api-package-integration-collaboration-same-object-two-states.md`. That file remains the starting point for review, preserving the incident as observed and its attachments rather than a reorganized integration guide. The recovery page preserves the fact that recovery occurred; the supplementary note on the unconfirmed cause preserves the unresolved parts. The three sets of material can be cross-referenced, but each has a different temporal context.

The conclusion in the earlier record that "recovery is possible within the compatibility window" has not been deleted. At the time, it resolved the question of whether the user flow could continue working through a compatibility combination, rather than declaring that the objects were already consistent. The public entry point failure added later showed precisely that the recovery conclusion had a narrower scope than it initially appeared to have.

The first review also revealed a wording issue: the earlier record placed the result seen by the caller alongside the current revision seen at the entry point, making it read like a direct comparison. In fact, the material only supports "the two were inconsistent"; no intermediate records were retained that were sufficient to show at which internal stage the difference arose. Therefore, this version does not rewrite this as a claim that a particular module had definitively produced an incorrect state.

## Observation window

Later cards clarified the changes over time, but did not provide a complete explanation of the cause. The table below lists only the points at which actions or comments were recorded. Periods not shown are not assumed to have been stable, nor are they assumed to have been free of anomalies.

| Point in time | Recorded facts | What could be determined from them at the time |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-02-20 | The assignee for IGTD-004 changed because the work mainly involved modifying the core module for api package integration collaboration | This work was still being adjusted, so the entry point's state at the time could not be treated as its final state |
| 2026-02-23 | The daily report merged two execution records, but the original card did not | The summary display was inconsistent with the original card's records, so the two records needed to be revisited separately |
| 2026-02-26 | IGTD-001 recorded qa_reproduced, then moved to In Progress | The observed situation was reproduced at that point; the action label did not provide the reproduction conditions |
| 2026-02-26 | The supplemental note pointed out that the collection record corresponding to the execution record had not arrived at all | "One segment is zero after merging" is not a reliable explanation, and what is missing is the collection-side record |
| 2026-03-02 | IGTD-004 began addressing the daily report merge issue | The merged row was treated as a separate issue, rather than dismissed as a display detail |
| 2026-03-02 | The merged daily report row was split back into two execution records, and the original card links were restored | The display was restored to two records, and the original card for each record could once again be located |
| 2026-03-02 | IGTD-007 began reproducing the two versions of the records | The subsequent review treated version differences as a separate subject |
| 2026-03-02 | Local results recovered; the public entry point corresponding to the exit entry point still failed | Recovery covered only local observations, and the public entry point still needed to be retained as an unrecovered path |

A section of the timeline is deliberately left unfilled. The qa_reproduced for IGTD-001 only indicates that a reproduction occurred, not which version combination the person reproducing it used, nor whether the public entry point had already failed at that time. The reproduction work on IGTD-007 likewise provided only the final observations: local recovery, public entry point still failing. Expanding these action labels into complete test conditions would fabricate evidence that does not exist.

The daily report issue in IGTD-004 also cannot be reduced to a "display fix". When the daily report combined two execution records into one row, the original card did not contain that merged record, so readers could not tell whether the row represented one execution, two executions, or a summary produced after a gap in data collection. Splitting it back into two records and restoring the original card links later addressed a break in traceability: readers could once again navigate from the summary row to each original record. This fix did not establish why the collection records had not arrived.

## The impact is not a straight line

For consumers, the most direct impact is that they cannot determine the integration configuration from old records alone. If old records, the current entry point, and evidence from callers point in different directions, consumers face two risks: first, mistaking a recoverable compatibility window for a stable state; second, mistaking a public entry point that is still failing for one that has recovered. No material was retained from this incident that would allow the number of affected consumers to be counted, so no figures or scope are added here.

For maintainers, the impact is that the order of assessment has changed. Previously, if they looked at the daily report's summary row first, the merged row would compress two executions into one; if they then looked at local results, a return to green could obscure the fact that the public entry point had not recovered. The situation cannot be characterized based on the last output that appears normal; the entry point, original card, execution records, and public entry point must each be placed back at their respective observation points.

For the exit window, recovery and exit are not the same determination. After the compatibility window recovers, the user path can continue, but if the public entry point associated with the exit entry point is still failing, that does not justify declaring that the current object has completed its exit. The operational details of the exit window checklist are maintained in DOC-43; this page retains only why, in this incident, "local recovery" cannot be directly recorded as "exit complete".

For the original record, the impact is that historical assessments must not be silently overwritten. The original record is valuable not because it provides the final answer, but because it preserves the inputs from a time when two states had not yet been consolidated into a single account. Subsequent recovery, the splitting of the daily report records, and the public entry point failure should all be appended as additional material, rather than going back and rewriting the original observations into a single conclusion.

## Steps taken at the time to narrow things down

The first step to narrow things down was to save the original input and entry point version, and stop further retries. The aim was to preserve what was seen at the first deviation from the baseline. This did not resolve the issue, but it prevented later recovery results from being mistakenly placed in the initial observation window.

The second step to narrow things down was to separate the time of recovery from the time of cause confirmation. After the compatibility window recovered, "recovery" was not recorded as "cause confirmed" during the incident. This made it possible to retain an uncomfortable but accurate status afterward: the user path had recovered, but why the replay records had changed was still unknown.

The third step to narrow things down took place in the daily report records. The merged row was split back into two execution records, and the original card links were restored. After the split, it could be confirmed that the daily report had previously lost the ability to distinguish the two records; what could not be confirmed was whether this merge was part of the same causal chain as the collection records not arriving, the entry point revision differences, or the public entry point failure.

The fourth step to narrow things down was to document the local results and the public entry point separately. While the public entry point was still failing, the local recovery was neither retracted nor used to overwrite the public entry point's result. The results of the two paths need to be retained separately until there is material showing that they agree under the same version combination.

None of these actions is a complete remediation plan. They only prevent the situation on the ground from being swallowed by a larger narrative. The cross-package dependencies, version combinations, and consumer integrations involving api-package-integration still need to be checked separately; this page has not rewritten them as an internal failure of a single service.

## Explanations That Were Once Insufficient

"The caller's evidence differs from the old record" was initially easy to interpret as meaning that the old record had expired. That interpretation was too quick. The old record described the entry point and original input it had saved at the time; the current entry point provided a different current revision at another point in time, which does not automatically invalidate the old material. The actual shortcoming of the old material was that it did not explain what happened between the two observation points.

"The merged daily-report row is simply zero" was also disproved by later material. The addendum explicitly states that this part was not zero; the collection record corresponding to the execution record never arrived at all. Writing a missing record as zero would disguise a collection problem as a normal empty result and obscure why the daily report ended up with only one row.

"Local recovery indicates that the integration has recovered" was likewise insufficient. The results for IGTD-007 directly showed the opposite combination: the local result recovered, while the public endpoint corresponding to the exit entry point was still failing. This difference does not need to be rhetorically turned into a complex failure; it only needs to be recorded as two paths.

"There was likewise no basis for saying that the event ended after the daily report was split back into two entries." Splitting it back into two entries and restoring the link to the original card restored the conditions for looking up each item individually, but did not explain why the collection record was late, missing, or never arrived. Nor did it explain why the old entry point and current entry point showed different current revisions at the two observation points.

Therefore, this version does not describe this incident as "identified" or "eliminated." What has happened is the record split, local recovery, the continued failure of the public endpoint, and the recovery of the compatibility window; what has not happened is attributing these phenomena to a verified root cause.

## Original Card and Verification Entry Points

Each related card preserves a different small piece of the incident evidence and should not substitute for one another.

- IGTD-001 left requirements to save the exit code before releasing the current revision, coordinate on api package integration, and retain the final segment of the logs, and qa_reproduced later appeared together with an in-progress action. It was the entry point used to save the final output at the time.
- IGTD-004 recorded the fixed api-package-integration, the current entry and command, and the comparison intent of replacing only the current revision; subsequent materials also documented the process of merging the daily report, splitting it into two execution records, and restoring the original card link.
- IGTD-007 focused on non-author reproduction of the records from the two versions. The final observation was not that everything passed, but that the local result was restored while the public entry still failed.
- IGTD-009 was associated with the resource-return window registration for the current revision. It can help review how the exit window was registered at the time, but it does not provide the reason for the difference in the current status.
- IGTD-010 focused on the differences after a cold start of the current entry and required clearing one's own cache first without touching the shared cache. This card serves as a local entry point for later comparison of entry differences; it should not be used to assert that the cache is the cause.

The only thing these cards have in common is that they are all near the current object. They do not constitute a complete diagnostic report. In particular, the cold-start comparison in IGTD-010 only indicates that the current entry after a cold start needs to be compared; it cannot thereby designate the shared cache as the fault point; the return-window registration in IGTD-009 only indicates that the exit action needs to record a time boundary, and cannot thereby explain the public entry failure.

The review order therefore remains: first open the original event record and confirm the entry and input retained at the time; then, as needed, return to the original cards to inspect their respective local observations; finally, compare the local path, public entry, and daily report record across different points in time. If any step reveals that only a summary result remains, with no original card link, or that only a recovery page remains, with no original context, that is insufficient to replace the preceding step.

```text
Caller evidence
    │
    ├── Observations in old records
    │
Current entry ── current revision at the two observation points
    │
Daily report summary ── merged line ── split back into two execution records ── original card link
    │
Local result ── restored
Public entry ── still failing
```

The diagram does not show an arrow from the daily report to the public entry point, nor an arrow from the current revision to the collection record. This is not an omission: the existing materials do not confirm these directions. The diagram retains only known parallel relationships, to avoid readers misreading adjacent items as causal relationships that have already been established.

## Things that must still be distinguished after recovery

The recovery page is worth retaining because it records that the compatibility window is recoverable. This is an important status for integrators: within that window, the user path no longer retains its initial anomalous result. However, the compatibility window being recoverable does not mean all consumers have completed the switch, nor does it mean that the exit entry on the public path has recovered.

Local recovery is likewise worth retaining because it narrows the scope of what is still failing. It cannot replace the result from the public entry point. An integrator seeing a normal local result cannot therefore skip the public entry point; a maintainer seeing a failure at the public entry point should not write it back as though local recovery had never occurred. The two records have different operational value.

The two execution records resulting from splitting the daily report must also still be retained. Once the merged row is corrected, readers can revisit the original card for each record, rather than infer the process from a one-line summary. The fact that the collection record was not received should continue to be preserved as an unconfirmed item: it is currently unknown when or why this happened, or whether it originated from the same source as the entry-point discrepancy.

The two observation points for the current revision should likewise not be overwritten by a later recovery event. They are the starting point of this incident. As long as the change between the two observation points remains unexplained, "the same object gave different current revision values at two points in time" must still be treated as an observed fact from the incident, not as outdated wording.

## Remaining unconfirmed items

The following questions remain open because the existing materials support only the questions themselves, not their answers.

1. At which observation points were the two current revision values observed, respectively, and what changes between them can be confirmed.
2. Why was the collection record corresponding to the execution record not received; did the daily-report merge merely expose this gap.
3. Did local recovery and the continued failure at the public entry point occur under the same version combination and the same integration conditions.
4. Which consumer integrations did the compatibility-window recovery cover, and which exit conditions remain unmet.
5. Can the current entry-point discrepancy after a cold start be reproduced as the same phenomenon as the earlier entry-point discrepancy.

These questions are not a substitute for action items. They record the boundaries this retrospective was unable to close. If new input is obtained later, it should be appended after the corresponding observation point and state whether it changes the entry-point state, execution-record state, path state, or recovery state; do not directly fold the new material back into the original wording of the old record.

## Stop points when using this record later

If you only have one merged line from the daily report, first return to the two split execution records and the links to the original cards; if both cannot be obtained, do not use this to assess the execution process.

If you only see recovery of the compatibility window, first confirm whether that recovery was seen in the local result or at the public entry point; when recovery has not appeared in both places simultaneously, do not treat it as full integration recovery.

If you only see one result for the current entry point, first confirm which observation point it corresponds to; if the saved content from the other point in time is unavailable, do not use a single result to overwrite the old record.

If the review can only obtain the recovery page, stop at the observation "Recovered"; do not add an explanation for why the replay records changed. The recovery page does not provide evidence about the cause.

If you find that a consumer failed to connect but the version combination and entry state were not retained, do not use this incident to directly assign the same cause either. What is recorded here is one specific anomaly involving api-package-integration, not a template for all cross-package integration failures.

## Record Maintenance Method

The original file continues to preserve the incident scene and attachments: `docs/adj-api/incidents/api-package-integration-collaboration-same-object-two-states.md`. When updating it, prioritize appending new observations, correcting explanations previously proven inaccurate, or restoring the missing original-card entry; do not delete the "cause unknown" portion from the old version merely to make the narrative orderly.

DOC-43 maintains the operational checklist for the exit window. This page points to it only when it is necessary to determine "whether recovery is sufficient to exit"; it does not copy the checklist contents. In this way, the incident materials retain why local recovery is insufficient to represent recovery of the public entry point, while the exit-window materials retain the specific execution items.

The most valuable thing retained this time is not a polished conclusion, but several facts that cannot cover for one another: the entry point gave different current revision values at two points in time; the daily report merged two execution records; the corresponding collection record did not arrive; the daily report later split the records and restored the original card; the public entry point still failed after local recovery; the compatibility window could recover. Together, they describe the outline of the anomaly, but they still do not constitute a verifiable single cause.

When reviewing this again next time, start with one fact from this set that is directly relevant to the question at that time, rather than first assuming that all states have already synchronized.

# Freeze Boundary FAQ

This page collects the questions we kept coming back to in three discussions. We've started with how we handled them at the time; candidate paths and the final window weren't recorded separately.

## What can the merge-base entry point tell us?

It can show that two sets of refs can be compared starting from the same Merge Baseline. At the time, we treated this result as grounds for freezing a candidate: if the entry point could still return a base, we considered the candidate path to still be within the window. This was mainly to avoid having to revisit every merge context during review.

## Who withdraws candidate paths?

The original proposer crosses it out in the record first; if a second person thinks the path shouldn't enter the window, they can also withdraw it directly. There's no separate handoff step. It's easy here to treat "proposing a candidate" and "confirming a freeze" as the same thing, but we didn't set out a separate boundary at the time.

## When can it be closed?

Post the result of merge-base in chat, and if no one continues to propose a different path, treat it as closed. If it turns out later that the baseline has changed, just reopen this item.

If the minimal repro record is missing, leave a question mark for now; we hadn't agreed at the time on how much needed to be filled in.

# Freeze Boundary FAQ

This page was originally used to explain whether candidate paths should stay or go. The wording took a shortcut: once merge-base returned a result, it tied comparison, withdrawal, and closure together. After review, that wording is still in the history above, but it can no longer be used on its own to determine the window's status.

## What can the merge-base entry point tell us?

It can only provide a Merge Baseline for comparing refs. If the entry point exists and can return a base, this comparison still has a reference point; it does not confirm that a candidate path is frozen. The earlier answer, "if a base can be found, it's within the window," treated a code entry point as a team decision. When you find the entry point, you can record the refs and base you see, but don't use them as a substitute for reviewing the candidate path.

This is especially easy to misread during a merge: a path may still be comparable, yet no longer suitable as a window candidate. The old answer didn't address this distinction; it's retained only to explain why we originally conflated the two.

## Who withdraws candidate paths?

The original draft said the original proposer or a second reviewer could cross it out directly. The review did not establish this as a stable ownership rule, so that statement can't be treated as the withdrawal entry point. Decisions on keeping or dropping a candidate path should stay on the corresponding surface; when withdrawing a path, just record the path and the reason. There is still no answer for cases with a missing minimal repro record. Log those as unknown first; don't fill the gap with a judgment from a single chat.

## When can it be closed?

"No objections" in chat no longer counts as a closure condition. An item can only be closed after someone other than the author reruns it through the same entry point and confirms the rollback observations for the release or incident. Unconfirmed items stay on the corresponding surface; a chat conclusion must not override long-term documentation.

This also explains why output from merge-base alone isn't enough: it can provide a clue for a rerun, but it doesn't cover rollback observations. If the person rerunning it gets a different candidate path, keep the difference for now; don't carry the earlier closed status over to the new path.

# On-Call Handoff Decision Memo

This Northstar Developer Tools review began with a specific handoff problem: on-call staff can see the behavior around the stream-lines entry point, but may not know whether a given action is an agreed response or a suggestion still awaiting confirmation from the module owner. Keeping all of this in one place may seem convenient, but the next shift can easily mistake a recovery action for a root-cause finding, or treat a tentative assessment in chat as long-term guidance.

This review did not try to expand the handoff material into a complete incident record. The goal of the decision was to let the person taking over answer three questions first: what has been decided in this round; where to find the repository inputs and raw outputs supporting the assessments; and which views remain unresolved and must not become conclusions simply by being handed over.

## Decisions Made

Keep the existing stream-lines entry point while adjusting the handoff boundary of the Integrity Window. The entry point itself will not move; the window will include only assessments supported by the evidence already available. This does not make the window a boundary for technical root causes. It limits what can be explicitly passed on during handoff. Anything not yet reproduced, lacking raw output, or without an identified module owner stays outside the window and must be explicitly marked as pending confirmation.

Every handoff must retain at least two types of material: inputs reproducible in the repository, and the raw outputs produced by those inputs. Use these first to establish the scope of the observed behavior, then discuss whether a rollback is needed and whether a direction for a fix has already been identified. An issue name, a secondhand error report, or a post-recovery state alone cannot replace this pair of materials.

A rollback can reduce impact, but it cannot replace root-cause confirmation. The inputs, outputs, and unresolved assessments from the time should still be retained after recovery. Otherwise, the next shift will know only that "it recovered at one point," without being able to distinguish whether the discrepancy came from the entry point, the parsing results, or a module further downstream.

## Approaches Considered

The first approach was to keep both the existing entry point and the previous, less restrictive handoff process. Its advantage was that on-call staff would not need to change where they looked, and clues already raised in chat could be forwarded quickly. The problem was that tentative clues would be mixed with confirmed decisions: an observation might lack reproducible input, and a rollback might be mistaken for evidence that the issue had been located. This approach was not adopted as the handoff rule.

The second approach was to adjust the Integrity Window so that only items with both pieces of evidence retained could enter the handoff. This adds preparation work and means some seemingly valuable hypotheses cannot yet be written into long-term conclusions. In return, the person taking over can tell which items can be rerun and which are still waiting. The review chose this approach and retained the existing stream-lines entry point as the place for discovery and collection.

One proposal was to trace all relevant calls through to final attribution before handing over the material. This was not adopted. It would make confirmed root cause a prerequisite for handoff, holding up the on-call shift change while a response from the responsible module was still pending. Another proposal was to record only whether the rollback succeeded. That can show whether impact decreased, but not whether the original behavior disappeared, and it does not leave enough material for later attribution.

## What Goes in Each of the Three Records

Board records only the status, the responsible owner, and the next step. It should tell the person taking over where things stand, without carrying the full reasoning. A status change must not erase the fact that the root cause remains unconfirmed.

Docs stores reusable guidance for each version, including this decision, the applicable evidence boundary, and the assessments that should be replaced if corrections are made later. Long-term documentation must distinguish the approved scope from reservations, rather than turning the on-call chat into a smooth narrative.

Chat retains observations, waits, and referrals from the time. It is suitable for quickly adding the location of raw output, explaining that a module owner has not yet taken ownership, or retracting a hypothesis contradicted by later material. Chat content can help point to where to look next, but it does not automatically become a decision.

These are not three copies of the same record. Board focuses on whether the action at hand can move forward; Docs focuses on assessments that can be reused later; Chat focuses on the situation at the time, before it has been consolidated into a lasting record. Copying the same conclusion verbatim into all three will only create more discrepancies when corrections are needed later.

## What Must Be Clear at Handoff

A handoff entry should state this round's decision first, then attach the corresponding reproducible inputs and raw outputs. If a rollback has been performed, make clear that it changed the impact status, rather than presenting it as confirmation of the root cause. If an assessment still depends on confirmation from a module owner, retain its conditions and where it has been referred; do not compress it into "handled."

Brief clues may be retained for material outside the window, but they must not be used to expand the approved scope. For example, if all that is known is that some behavior occurs alongside the stream-lines entry point, with no stable input or raw output yet available, simply record that it is waiting. Do not specify a direction for a fix on that basis, or require the next shift to treat it as an established fact.

## Reservations

This decision does not establish that the issue necessarily occurs at the entry point, nor that adjusting the Integrity Window will eliminate later discrepancies. The window addresses the mixing of evidence during handoff; it is not an alternative explanation of the technical cause. If later material shows that the behavior originates in another module, the long-term guidance should be amended. This decision still retains its scope and rationale as they stood at the time.

The review also required that records not be closed on the basis of "rollback succeeded." Post-rollback observations should continue to be retained alongside the original inputs and outputs until the corresponding module completes attribution, or new material clearly overturns the original boundaries of the observed behavior. This allows on-call handoffs to proceed without presenting unconfirmed assessments as completed work.

# Freeze Boundary Switchover Handoff Notes

Treat this switchover as a migration, not an entry point rename. The handoff covers the Integrity Window freeze boundary. The material we can confirm at this point comes from path-safety's known consumers, old entry points, and candidate paths.

Before the switchover, list each known consumer and record the old entry point it actually uses. Neither listing names alone nor filling gaps with alternative evidence that looks compatible counts as confirmation. Have one consumer that can roll back on its own try the candidate path first; leave the other consumers on the old entry point for the time being.

The handoff record must include at least the revision, a minimal reproduction, the first divergence, and a next-step entry point. The revision pins down what is being reviewed; the minimal reproduction must let the person taking over see the same divergence again; the first divergence identifies where the two paths first differ; the next-step entry point must allow execution to continue. If either the caller population or the rollback action is missing, keep the page marked as migration in progress.

On rollback, restore the original entry point and preserve the divergence that led to the rollback. Board records status and next steps, Docs holds the long-term guidance, and Chat is only for live observations, pending items, or referrals; all three link back to the same event. DOC-01 can still serve as local reference material around the old entry point.

# Frozen-Boundary Switchover Handoff Guide

This page initially described the handoff as "switching entry points", but it later became clear that what actually needed to be frozen was the boundary: who is using path-safety, who still depends on the old entry point, and where the candidate path first differs from the old path. The old steps have not been deleted, because they explain why migration involving multiple parties was initially arranged as a single linear sequence; the handoff must now proceed within scopes that can be verified and rolled back locally.

```text
Old entry point ──Confirm the consumer and entry point──> Select one consumer that can roll back
   │                              │
   │                              ├─ revision
   │                              ├─ Minimal reproduction
   │                              └─ First divergence
   │                                      │
   └────────────Keep the old path───────── Explainable / Unconfirmed
                                          │       │
                                      Next batch    Restore the old entry point
```

## The Old Path Retained from the Initial Draft

When the initial draft was written, the easiest approach to execute was to list all known consumers together, then make the candidate path the unified entry point for the next version. This approach omitted the mapping to old entry points. If only consumer names are recorded, whoever takes over cannot determine which boundary each consumer actually crossed; if only the candidate path is recorded, they will not know which old path to restore after a failure.

Consumers and old entry points must therefore be retained in pairs. Each pair must correspond to at least one revision and include a minimal reproduction. The revision pins down the target examined in this review, while the minimal reproduction lets whoever takes over later observe the same state again. When the materials are incomplete, use Fang Ke to keep the status unknown, but do not infer from results in adjacent projects that it is ready to migrate.

An earlier, broader judgment was also retained: migration could continue as long as the candidate path appeared compatible. This judgment was later narrowed. An appearance of compatibility cannot substitute for the caller population, the first divergence, and the ability to roll back. The old wording remains in the historical section as the working assumption at the time; it no longer determines the scope of the next batch of consumers.

## The Card Produced by the First Review

After the review, the handoff no longer recorded only a status, but instead recorded the pieces that could be matched against one another separately.

| Field | Observed state to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Consumer | Confirmed callers; explicitly leave them unknown when they cannot be identified |
| Old entry point | The entry point this consumer currently depends on in practice |
| revision | The target version pinned down for this review |
| Minimal reproduction | The smallest set of materials that can reproduce the divergence |
| First divergence | The first point that differs after moving from the old entry point to the candidate path |
| Entry point for the next step | An entry point where whoever takes over can actually continue |
| Rollback action | An action that lets this consumer restore the old entry point on its own |

The field order is not a formatting preference. Without first pinning down the old entry point and revision, the minimal reproduction may refer to the wrong target; without the first divergence, it is impossible to determine what the candidate path actually changed; without a rollback action, a single trial run cannot be expanded into a migration batch. Fields may remain empty temporarily, but they must be marked as unconfirmed, not filled with a nearby piece of supporting material.

The first trial run of the candidate path remains limited to a single consumer. This consumer must be able to roll back on its own, not because it represents all callers, but because, when the first failure occurs, the impact will still be confined to one local boundary. Other known consumers continue to use their old entry points until the divergence is explained or the handoff is explicitly halted. A single success covers only the actual trial target, not the remaining targets automatically.

## The Misreading in the Intermediate Version

An intermediate version described "actual review" as meaning the candidate path had already been confirmed. Looking back, what had actually been confirmed was only one local trial run and its supporting materials, which could not be extended into permission to migrate all consumers. The current record therefore separates two things: a trial run can produce an operational result; for the migration to be complete, the caller population, old entry point, revision, minimal reproduction, first divergence, and rollback action must also match up.

Handling of the different cases also starts here. If the caller population is unknown, first return to the consumer inventory; if the revision is missing, first fill in the review target; if the minimal reproduction is not reproducible, the candidate path does not enter the next batch; if the rollback action is unavailable, the trial run itself does not meet the handoff requirements. If the first divergence is unexplained, the entry point for the next step can only point to materials for further investigation of the divergence or a place to take over, and cannot directly specify switching the remaining consumers.

These are not different conclusions, but different stopping points. They indicate whether the problem lies with the target, reproduction, path differences, the subsequent entry point, or the ability to restore. Only by recording which item the process has stopped at can those who follow know what to investigate next, rather than interpreting a single "success" as meaning all boundaries have been cleared.

## Trial Failure and Batch Progression

When a trial run fails, the consumer restores its original old entry point and retains the first divergence observed before the failure and the revision used at the time. Restoring the old entry point does not mean deleting the candidate path; the candidate path is still retained as material for the unfinished migration until a new review can explain the divergence. If the restoration action itself is not recorded, the page returns to migration in progress rather than being marked as rollback complete.

Only if the first divergence can be explained and the rollback action is still available should the next batch of candidate consumers be recorded. Each consumer in the next batch must still have its old entry point and review target recorded, and these fields cannot be omitted just because the previous batch succeeded. If the caller list changes, first update the inventory, then decide whether to continue; a previous "known" designation cannot be reused as a new confirmation result.

## Roles of the Three Record Locations

Board retains only the status, current stopping point, and next step. It does not duplicate the entire minimal reproduction or present pending questions as decided matters. Docs maintains the long-term, versioned account: why the old steps are retained, the current handoff sequence, the conditions for advancing batches, and the rollback criteria. Chat records only observations made at the time, whose confirmation is pending, and where a referral is needed; a chat comment that something "should be compatible" cannot be promoted to a documented conclusion.

The three locations can link back to one another, but the links must refer to the same event. You cannot write on Board that the switch to the candidate path is complete, write in Docs that it is still awaiting confirmation, and then piece together a third state using a success screenshot from Chat. Pass only the minimum content needed to convey entry points, statuses, or observations between these locations, and leave the long-term account for the handoff cards in Docs. DOC-01 provide localized rechecks around the old entry point and are related to this page, but do not replace the consumer inventory or migration decisions.

## Current Handoff Section

Before starting a migration batch, put the known consumers together with each one's old entry point, revision, minimal reproduction, first divergence, actionable entry point for the next step, and action for rolling back independently into a single record. Try the candidate path with one selected consumer first. Once observation is complete, expand the scope only if the divergence can be explained and the rollback action is available; if any item is unconfirmed, keep the migration in progress and stop at the corresponding field.

The current goal is not to move all consumers at once, but to make it possible to recheck the frozen boundary and restore just one location on failure. The trial results for the candidate path cover only the actual trial target, and the remaining targets still need to be confirmed one by one using their own old entry points.

Retained old examples:

- Old example A: Lists only the candidate path, not the old entry point. This is obsolete, and cannot be used as the basis for starting the switchover.
- Old example B: Expands directly to all consumers after one successful trial run. This is obsolete, and the scope of success still extends only to the target of that trial run.

If the entry point for the next step, first divergence, or rollback action is not clearly documented, the handoff stops here.
